[HEADING-H2] Who gets paid? Understanding payees and how they work in financial transactions
[HEADING-H3] Understanding payees in financial transactions
[PARAGRAPH] Payees play a critical role in financial transactions by receiving payments in exchange for goods or services. As a key participant, it’s important to understand what a payee is and their function when money changes hands.
[PARAGRAPH] A payee refers to the party on the receiving end of a payment within a financial transaction. Also known as the recipient, the payee is the individual or business to whom payment is made. For instance, when you purchase groceries at the supermarket, the grocery store is the payee.
[PARAGRAPH] Or if you take your car to the auto shop for repairs, the auto repair shop is the payee. In both cases, you are the payer providing money and the grocery store and auto shop are the payees receiving the funds.
[HEADING-H3] Types of payees
[PARAGRAPH] Payees can be people or organizations of all types and sizes. Some common examples of payees include:
[LIST-ITEM] Retail stores and service providers – Any business you patronize as a customer is a payee when you exchange money for products or services. This includes grocery stores, restaurants, gas stations, department stores, auto mechanics, doctors offices, etc.
[LIST-ITEM] Landlords – If you rent a home or apartment, your landlord is the payee who receives rental payments from you every month.
[LIST-ITEM] Lenders – Banks, credit card companies, mortgage companies, and other lending institutions are payees when you send them loan payments.
[LIST-ITEM] Contractors and freelancers – When you hire contractors like electricians, plumbers, lawyers, and consultants they are payees who receive payment from you upon completion of work.
[LIST-ITEM] Friends and family – If you owe money to friends or family members, they become the payee when you pay them back.
[LIST-ITEM] Government entities – The IRS and other government bodies are payees when you submit tax payments or pay fees.
[LIST-ITEM] Charities – Nonprofit organizations and charities are payees when they receive donations from donors and supporters. No matter the type of transaction, the payee’s role remains the same – to receive the payment amount in exchange for an item purchased or service rendered.
[PARAGRAPH] As the recipient of funds, payees must provide invoices, account numbers, or payment information to clearly identify wheremoney should be sent. Proper payee identification ensures payments go to the correct party and are accounted for properly.
[HEADING-H3] The bottom line
[PARAGRAPH] Understanding the meaning and function of a payee is useful when examining any type of financial transaction. Payees represent a core component of money changing hands in an economy. Whether you’re the one making a payment or receiving it as the designated payee, being familiar with this key term is essential.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Full Retirement Sum (FRS)?
[PARAGRAPH] By the age of 55, there are three savings targets linked to your CPF Retirement Sum that you can aim to achieve. Depending on which target you reach, your retirement payouts will be categorised as follows:
[PARAGRAPH] The CPF Retirement Sum refers to the complete sum of your CPF savings that should be allocated to ensure a comfortable retirement lifestyle. Upon reaching age 65, monthly payouts will be provided and will persist throughout your lifetime.
[PARAGRAPH] These sums represent the amount you should set aside in your Retirement Account (RA) by age 55 to ensure a certain level of monthly payouts during your retirement years.
[PARAGRAPH] The Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) serves as the minimum threshold, while the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) provide higher payout levels.
[HEADING-H2] How does the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) work?
[PARAGRAPH] If you meet the FRS target but do not own any property, you can withdraw either S$5,000 or any amount exceeding the FRS in your account, whichever is greater.
[PARAGRAPH] However, if you are a property owner and meet the FRS, you can withdraw any amount exceeding the BRS present in your RA.
[PARAGRAPH] Typically, the FRS is twice the amount of the BRS, ensuring you can withdraw at least half of the funds available in your account.
[HEADING-H2] What should I know about the CPF Retirement Sum?
[PARAGRAPH] Keep in mind that you have flexibility when it comes to the Retirement Sums.
[PARAGRAPH] You are not obligated to strictly adhere to the prescribed BRS, FRS, or ERS. Regardless of the specific amounts, you can still receive lifelong income based on the CPF savings you have accumulated by age 55.
[PARAGRAPH] In fact, you may even be exempted partially or entirely from the Retirement Sums if you are enrolled in a lifelong pension scheme or have a private annuity plan. However, it’s important to note that such exemptions are subject to approval from the CPF Board, and specific criteria must be met.
[PARAGRAPH] The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, head over to the official website.

[HEADING-H2] What is negotiation in real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] Negotiation is the process of agreeing on the terms of a property deal between a buyer and a seller. This includes discussions about the offer, covering the price, timelines, conditions, and things that come with the property.
[PARAGRAPH] The goal is to reach terms that both parties find acceptable.
[HEADING-H2] What are some key aspects of negotiation in real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] Key aspects of this negotiation involve agreeing on the property’s price, negotiating closing costs like taxes and fees, deciding on conditions (contingencies) that must be met, discussing items that come with the property (like appliances or furniture), and sometimes even negotiating the commission fees for real estate agents.
[HEADING-H2] How to negotiate for the best real estate deals?
[PARAGRAPH] Whether you’re a first-time homebuyer or an experienced real estate investor, honing your negotiation skills can potentially save you thousands of dollars. Here are seven savvy tips to help you navigate and master the art of negotiating in the property market.
[PARAGRAPH] Get pre-approved for a mortgage: Demonstrating financial readiness is crucial. Obtain pre-approval for a mortgage to show sellers that you are a serious and capable buyer. Armed with a pre-approval letter, you not only exhibit commitment but also highlight the maximum loan amount you can secure, aiding in negotiations.
[PARAGRAPH] Know the seller’s situation: Investigate the seller’s motivations for listing the property. Understanding their circumstances, such as job changes, family growth, or retirement, can provide insight into their flexibility regarding offers. Tailor your negotiation strategy based on their urgency and needs.
[PARAGRAPH] Make a strong first offer: Your initial offer sets the tone for negotiations. Offer a competitive price, aiming for 5-10% below the listing price if justified by your research. Provide evidence supporting the offer’s reasonableness, signalling your genuine interest in making a fair deal.
[PARAGRAPH] Be ready to negotiate and compromise: Anticipate counteroffers and be prepared for a back-and-forth exchange. Identify areas where you can compromise, such as agreeing to the seller’s closing date or leaseback options. Define your non-negotiables and be willing to make concessions within your limits to facilitate a successful deal.
[PARAGRAPH] Bring in an experienced real estate agent: Enlist the expertise of a skilled real estate agent to represent your interests. A knowledgeable agent can offer insights into the local market, craft effective proposals, and navigate negotiations. Rely on their experience to guide you through the process and secure favourable terms.
[PARAGRAPH] Trust your instincts: Listen to your intuition during negotiations. Trust your gut feelings about whether an offer is fair or unrealistic. Avoid being swayed by emotions and be prepared to walk away from a deal that doesn’t align with your standards. Additionally, scrutinise seemingly advantageous deals by inspecting the property for potential issues.
[PARAGRAPH] By following these tips, you can prepare yourself for successful real estate negotiations, making informed decisions and ultimately securing the keys to your dream property.

[HEADING-H2] What to do if the Subsidiary Certificate of Title is lost, damaged, or wrongfully withheld?

[HEADING-H2] What is Fiscal Policy?
[PARAGRAPH] Fiscal policy involves the utilisation of government expenditures and tax strategies to impact the overall economic situation, particularly broader factors like total demand for goods and services (GST), job availability, inflation, and economic expansion.
[PARAGRAPH] In times of economic downturn, the government might reduce tax percentages or enhance spending to stimulate demand and foster economic motion.
[PARAGRAPH] On the contrary, during instances of rising prices, it could heighten tax rates or decrease spending to moderate the pace of economic growth.
[HEADING-H2] How does the Fiscal Policy work in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore, the ongoing aims of fiscal policy include:
[LIST-ITEM] Nurturing and supporting steady economic growth without triggering inflation.
[LIST-ITEM] Keeping a balanced budget, which means funding all types of expenses – both day-to-day and developmental – with the money earned throughout different economic phases.
[LIST-ITEM] Directing government spending toward providing important public services and goods, like education, healthcare, infrastructure, housing, and projects dedicated to protecting the environment.

[HEADING-H2] HDB Season Parking: Everything you need to know
[PARAGRAPH] HDB season parking is a long-term parking solution for motorists, allowing them to park their vehicles at HDB car parks for a flat monthly rate. This service is ideal for residents or employees working in HDB precincts, providing convenience and flexibility. Here’s a comprehensive guide to how HDB season parking works, the application process, and the renewal options.
[HEADING-H2] What is HDB season parking?
[PARAGRAPH] HDB season parking allows motorists to park their vehicles at HDB car parks on a calendar month basis. It’s designed for long-term parking and is ideal for HDB residents or individuals working in HDB precincts. The parking can be renewed electronically, making it a convenient option for those who need consistent access to a parking space near their residence or workplace.
[HEADING-H2] HDB season parking rates
[PARAGRAPH] The rates for HDB season parking vary depending on several factors, including the type of vehicle (e.g., cars, motorcycles, commercial vehicles), the type of car park (e.g., sheltered or non-sheltered), and whether you are a resident or non-resident. The rates are categorised as:
[LIST-ITEM] Tier 1: Applicable to residents (flat owners, tenants, or registered occupants) for their first vehicle.
[LIST-ITEM] Tier 2: Applies to subsequent vehicles owned by residents or all vehicles owned by non-residents.
[HEADING-H2] How is HDB season parking allocated?
[PARAGRAPH] The allocation of HDB season parking is prioritised based on the demand at individual car parks. Here’s how it works:
[LIST-ITEM] 1st Priority: Reserved for HDB flat owners, tenants, and allowed occupants, ensuring they have the first right to apply for parking spaces. Applications open on the 1st of each month.
[LIST-ITEM] 2nd Priority: Applies to owners of second or subsequent vehicles. Applications for these vehicles begin on the 18th of each month.
[LIST-ITEM] 3rd Priority: For non-residents, tenants of rooms, and those applying for a vehicle they do not own. Applications open from the 21st of each month.
[PARAGRAPH] If the car park you are applying for is in high demand, you may not always secure a spot on your first attempt.
[HEADING-H2] How to apply for HDB season parking
[PARAGRAPH] You can apply for HDB season parking online through the HDB e-Service portal or the Mobile@HDB app. The process requires you to log in using your SingPass and fill in details related to your vehicle and preferred car park.
[PARAGRAPH] Payment can be made through Visa, MasterCard, or direct debit with DBS, UOB, OCBC, and Standard Chartered. Additional documents may be required if you are driving a company car or other commercial vehicles.
[HEADING-H2] Renewing HDB season parking
[PARAGRAPH] Renewal is also done online using the same e-Service portal or Mobile@HDB app. To avoid the hassle of missing renewals, you can set up automatic payments via GIRO, which offers a 2% rebate for successful transactions. If you prefer, you can also set up recurring credit card payments, which may come with benefits such as rewards points or cashback depending on your card provider.
[PARAGRAPH] Be sure to renew your parking promptly; otherwise, short-term parking charges will apply until your renewal is processed.
[HEADING-H2] Transferring and cancelling of HDB season parking
[PARAGRAPH] If you move or change vehicles, you can transfer your season parking using the “Permanent Transfer of Season Parking” e-Service. Note that the cost may vary based on the vehicle or car park type (e.g., from motorcycle to car or vice versa).
[PARAGRAPH] To cancel your season parking, you can do so after utilising it for at least one full month. HDB will refund you any unused portion of the parking fees for the remaining month(s). The cancellation process is also handled through the e-Service portal.

[HEADING-H2] What is Doing Business As (DBA)?
[PARAGRAPH] A Doing Business As (DBA) name signifies a title utilised by a company that differs from its officially registered business name. This enables businesses to conduct operations under a designated trade name for branding and promotional objectives while preserving their legal entity designation.
[PARAGRAPH] Securing registration for a DBA name is imperative for Singaporean businesses operating under a title distinct from their legal entity name to adhere to regulatory standards and safeguard their brand recognition.
[HEADING-H2] How to create a Doing Business As (DBA) in real estate that is memorable?
[PARAGRAPH] In the competitive real estate industry, having a strong brand identity is crucial for success. Your DBA name, or “Doing Business As” name, is a key component of your brand and should be carefully crafted to help you stand out. With some strategic thinking, you can develop a DBA name that maximises your visibility and memorability in the real estate market.
[PARAGRAPH] Your DBA name should reflect what makes your real estate business different and valuable compared to others. This could relate to your area of expertise, your approach to client relationships, or your niche market. For example, “The First-Time Home Buyer Specialists” immediately conveys an area of specialisation. “Your Neighborhood Realtors” communicates a local, relationship-driven approach. Take time to identify your competitive advantage and work it into your DBA name.
[PARAGRAPH] In an industry saturated with real estate agents, a forgettable or generic DBA name simply will not cut it. You need a name that is sticky in the minds of potential clients and stands out from the competition. Using alliteration, rhymes, puns, or unique word combinations can help with memorability. “Property Pros” has a catchy alliteration. “Home Sweet Home Realty” uses a rhyme and familiar phrase. Get creative brainstorming possibilities!
[PARAGRAPH] While you want your name to be memorable, don’t make it overly clever or complex. Real estate is based on relationships, so you want people to easily recall and pronounce your business name when recommending you to friends and family. Stay away from convoluted plays on words or obscure references. The clearer and simpler your DBA is, the better.
[PARAGRAPH] Once you have a few strong name candidates, check that the domain and social media handles are actually available before selecting your final DBA name. There is nothing more frustrating than falling in love with a name, only to find the .com has been taken since 1996. Do your research to ensure the name you want aligns with available web properties you can use to build your brand’s digital presence.
[PARAGRAPH] If you work under a larger real estate brokerage, check whether they have guidelines about agents using DBA names, and whether your proposed name needs approval. Some brokerages expressly prohibit DBA names to maintain consistent branding. Others allow it but have parameters around not including the brokerage name. Know the rules of your specific company.
[PARAGRAPH] Once you settle on your perfect DBA name, look into your state and local requirements for registering it as a legal business name. The filing process is typically very straightforward. Congratulations, you now have an exceptional DBA name to start building your standout real estate brand!

[HEADING-H2] What is a bungalow or detached house in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore, a detached house is often called a bungalow, regardless of whether it has one or multiple floors.
[PARAGRAPH] A detached house is an independent structure located within its land area, without any shared walls or roofs with neighbouring properties.
[PARAGRAPH] These houses are also one of the largest housing options available in Singapore. They are preferred because their walls are not attached to another property, providing residents with more privacy and exclusivity.
[HEADING-H2] What types of detached houses are there in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Detached houses in Singapore can take various forms and styles, including Colonial bungalows, also known as black-and-white houses, which may not be located in designated Good Class Bungalow (GCB) districts, as well as modern bungalows.
[PARAGRAPH] All of these types of houses are classified as detached houses in Singapore.
[HEADING-H2] What are Colonial bungalows or black-and-white houses?
[PARAGRAPH] The name “colonial house” comes from the dark timber beams and whitewashed walls that give these houses their distinctive appearance. Originally built and designed by the British in the 19th century, these houses were the homes of high-ranking government officials, judges, and wealthy businessmen.
[PARAGRAPH] Approximately 500 of these black and white houses exist today, mainly in locations like Seletar. Managed and preserved by the Singapore Land Authority (SLA), most houses are state-owned and rented out for commercial purposes, such as restaurants and businesses, with some reserved for residential stays.
[PARAGRAPH] These houses are highly sought after due to their limited supply and unique colonial-style architecture, which allows residents to live in a historic home with a rich heritage.
[PARAGRAPH] In addition to their design and historical appeal, colonial houses are known for their spaciousness, often rivalling the size of GCBs.
[PARAGRAPH] Some colonial houses can exceed 5,000 sq ft, with land areas of over 31,000 sq ft. These houses are typically two storeys high and feature large rooms, grand halls, spacious verandas, large windows, lush gardens, and sometimes even swimming pools.
[HEADING-H2] What are Good Class Bungalows (GCB)?
[PARAGRAPH] GCBs are considered the most prestigious and exclusive type of landed housing in Singapore, representing the highest standard in Singapore properties.
[PARAGRAPH] Two main features differentiate GCBs from bungalows: their size and location. GCBs must have a minimum site area of 1,400 sqm and a maximum site coverage of 40%.
[PARAGRAPH] To maintain their exclusivity and preserve their character and reputation, GCBs can only be constructed in 39 designated areas in Singapore. These locations include prime and popular neighbourhoods such as Chatsworth, Cluny Road near the Orchard Road shopping district, Ridley Park off Tanglin Road, Leedon Park near Holland Road, and King Albert Park off Bukit Timah Road.
[HEADING-H2] Semi-detached vs detached house – What’s the difference?
[PARAGRAPH] Typically, the main factor distinguishing between the two property types is how they are planned and built.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, a detached house is typically built as an independent structure within its land area, while a semi-detached house is commonly constructed next to a similar property and connected by a shared wall.

[HEADING-H2] What is Request for Proposal (RFP)?

[HEADING-H2] What is the caveat emptor?
[PARAGRAPH] The legal principle of “caveat emptor,” or “buyer beware,” means that if you were responsible for examining the property for defects before purchasing it, the Court would not intervene to save you from a bad deal.
[PARAGRAPH] It is crucial to remember that once you sign a contract in Singapore, you are legally bound by all of its terms.
[PARAGRAPH] If the contract includes an “as is, where is” clause, the Court will interpret this as your agreement to buy the property in its current state, regardless of whether or not you have examined it.
[PARAGRAPH] Since the contract states that you have accepted the property’s condition, it will be challenging to seek compensation from the seller if you discover any issues or flaws with the property.
[HEADING-H2] Must the seller inform me of any property defects?
[PARAGRAPH] In most situations, the seller is not obligated by law to inform the buyer about any property quality flaws that may impact its value. This regulation applies to both patent and latent defects.
[LIST-ITEM] Patent defects can be detected if the buyer is reasonably attentive during the property inspection. An example of such a defect is a large hole in the wall or visible water leaks. The law assumes that the buyer can identify such an obvious defect and raise concerns with the buyer.
[LIST-ITEM] Latent defects are problems with a property that cannot be expected to be discovered through a reasonable inspection. Under the principle of caveat emptor, a seller is not obligated to disclose latent defects in the quality of the property, even if they are aware of them.
[PARAGRAPH] However, if the seller fails to disclose existing defects when asked, they may be held responsible for misrepresentation, which would allow the buyer to cancel the contract and seek compensation for any damages incurred.
[PARAGRAPH] You assume responsibility for all defects in the property, regardless of whether they are easily noticeable or not. If you encounter defects after the purchase is finalised, you might have to consult a lawyer to determine if you have any legal options against the seller.
[PARAGRAPH] If you do not have any legal options, you might have to accept the property’s condition as is.
[HEADING-H2] What measures can you take as a buyer to protect your legal rights?
[PARAGRAPH] If you’re purchasing property under “as is where is” conditions, there are certain measures you can take to safeguard your legal rights as a buyer. Here are some tips:
[PARAGRAPH] During negotiations for your Option To Purchase (OTP), request the opportunity to conduct a second inspection of the property before finalising the purchase. If the seller agrees, hire reputable contractors or property inspectors to examine the entire property thoroughly. Including this clause in the OTP makes the seller less likely to allow the property to deteriorate from its initial condition.
[PARAGRAPH] You should also reserve the right to postpone the sale until the property is acceptable.
[PARAGRAPH] Take photos and videos during your initial inspection of the property to have evidence of its condition. This can be beneficial if legal action is needed to enforce your rights as a buyer. However, remember that such evidence may not be useful if you discover underlying structural issues or damage that was not visible during the inspection.
[PARAGRAPH] Most caveat emptor states mandate sellers to provide a property condition disclosure statement outlining known defects. Review this statement carefully and investigate any red flags. Verify permits for renovations to ensure compliance with building codes. Additionally, inspect the property at night to check for noise issues the seller may have omitted.
[PARAGRAPH] Title insurance safeguards against claims that could challenge your ownership of the property, such as legal claims by previous owners’ relatives. It covers legal expenses to defend your rights as the property owner and protects against errors in the title search process. Although it involves a one-time cost, title insurance provides invaluable peace of mind.
[PARAGRAPH] Make your offer contingent upon inspections and other due diligence processes to have an exit strategy if issues arise. Contingencies allow you to withdraw your offer and retrieve your earnest money deposit if the property fails to meet specific criteria. Common contingencies include financing, appraisal value, and inspection outcomes.
[PARAGRAPH] Collaborate with a knowledgeable real estate attorney and agent familiar with caveat emptor laws in your state. They can offer guidance on contingency language, required seller disclosures, and other protective measures. A competent agent will also possess extensive knowledge of the local market and potential red flags.
[PARAGRAPH] If something doesn’t feel right about the property or the seller’s disclosures, listen to your intuition. Request repairs or credits, or be prepared to walk away from the deal. Avoid succumbing to pressure to waive contingencies or inspections. Purchasing a “money pit” filled with hidden issues is never worthwhile. Stay objective – if significant problems arise, the home probably isn’t the right fit for you.

[HEADING-H2] What is Common Area Maintenance (CAM)?
[PARAGRAPH] Common Area Maintenance (CAM) is a crucial term in the world of real estate. It refers to the costs associated with maintaining common areas in a commercial property, such as lobbies, hallways, parking lots, and shared restrooms. These costs are typically borne by tenants in addition to their base rent, under the terms of their lease agreement.
[PARAGRAPH] If we consider a commercial building, the owner is responsible for its upkeep. However, the expenses incurred for maintaining the shared spaces are usually passed to the tenants. This is where CAM comes into play. It ensures that the shared spaces in a commercial building are well-maintained and functional, providing a clean and safe environment for everyone in the building.
[HEADING-H2] Calculating CAM and influencing factors
[PARAGRAPH] CAM charges are usually calculated on a pro-rata basis., meaning each tenant pays a portion of the total CAM costs proportional to the amount of space they lease in the building. For example, if a tenant leases 20% of the total leasable space in a building, they would be responsible for 20% of the total CAM costs.
[PARAGRAPH] Several factors influence CAM charges. These include the size of the leased space, the type of property, the location, and the specific terms of the lease agreement. Additionally, the actual costs of maintenance, repairs, and improvements to the common areas also play a significant role in the determining CAM charges.
[HEADING-H2] Comparing CAM with other real estate terms
[PARAGRAPH] CAM is often compared with other real estate terms like Operating Expenses and Additional Rent. While these terms might seem similar, they have distinct meanings. Operating Expenses include all costs associated with operating and maintaining a property, including property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs. CAM, on the other hand, specifically refers to the costs of maintaining common areas. Additional Rent refers to any expenses the tenant pays in addition to the base rent, which can include CAM charges, property taxes, and insurance costs.

[HEADING-H2] What is Ingress and Egress?
[PARAGRAPH] Ingress denotes the entitlement to enter a property, whereas egress signifies the right to exit. Collectively, ingress and egress encompass the legal privileges to access and depart from private property. These entitlements are linked to the ownership and utilisation of the property.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, tenants inhabiting an apartment possess the right to ingress and egress from the premises. The landlord cannot prevent the renters from entering or exiting as this forms part of their utilisation rights. Similarly, the landlord maintains ingress and egress privileges to reach the property for maintenance and repairs.
[HEADING-H2] Ingress and Egress easements
[PARAGRAPH] A prevalent method of establishing ingress and egress rights is through an easement. An easement entails the right to utilise or access another individual’s property for a specified purpose.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, if you own a landlocked piece of land lacking road access, you may acquire an ingress/egress easement from a neighbour. This would enable you to traverse a portion of their land to access your property. Easements can be granted in writing or may be established through historical usage and precedent.
[HEADING-H2] Emergency access rights
[PARAGRAPH] Crucially, government authorities possess the authority to enter private property without consent during emergency scenarios. This encompasses police officers, firefighters, and medical personnel responding to an emergency call. The right to breach property restrictions for emergency response aims to safeguard public health and safety.
[PARAGRAPH] Furthermore, utility workers often possess easement rights to access and repair electric, gas, water, and other utility lines, even on private property. This exception allows them to restore disrupted services that impact the community.
[HEADING-H2] Limits on Ingress and Egress rights
[PARAGRAPH] While ingress and egress rights are extensive, they are not without bounds. Reasonable restrictions may be imposed, provided they do not entirely impede access or exit from a property.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, gated communities may mandate guests to check-in before entry. Rental properties can establish basic regulations and hours for tenants accessing common areas. Additionally, private landowners may take suitable measures to prevent trespassers from unlawfully entering their property.
[PARAGRAPH] Nevertheless, restrictions designed to unlawfully target specific groups or individuals may contravene federal and state laws against discrimination.

[HEADING-H3] 2. Decoupling ownership
[HEADING-H3] 3. Purchase under a trust
[PARAGRAPH] Purchasing real estate under a trust for a child can help in avoiding ABSD if the recipient is a first-time purchaser. Setting up a trust for this method can be complicated, therefore it is advisable to consult a legal expert.
[HEADING-H3] 4. Sell existing property before purchasing another
[PARAGRAPH] Selling your current property before buying a new one can help you qualify as a first-time buyer and bypass ABSD. The timing is important because interim housing could be required while transitioning.
[HEADING-H3] 5. Invest in commercial properties
[PARAGRAPH] Buying commercial properties is an alternative investment strategy to avoid paying ABSD, which is applicable only to residential properties. Yet, investing in commercial properties carries its own risks and market factors.
[HEADING-H3] 6. Acquire dual-key units
[PARAGRAPH] Dual-key units provide owners with the flexibility of having two separate living spaces under one property title. This choice prevents paying ABSD for a subsequent purchase but comes with increased buying expenses and restricted availability.
[HEADING-H2] Risks and considerations
[PARAGRAPH] Every approach comes with unique financial and legal consequences. Consulting with property experts or legal advisors is vital to fully grasp these strategies and stay informed about any regulatory changes that might impact their effectiveness.
[HEADING-H2] Reasons to avoid ABSD
[PARAGRAPH] There are various grounds for steering clear of ABSD. Initially, the additional tax can create a significant financial hardship, particularly for property investors who are buying multiple properties.
[PARAGRAPH] ABSD affects the return on investment by lowering profits and raising exposure to market risks in case property values decrease. Real estate subject to ABSD might be challenging to sell fast due to increased expenses impacting its marketability.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Property buyers in Singapore can effectively strategize by legally avoiding or reducing ABSD, but it causes thorough planning and expert advice. Seeking advice from professionals can guarantee that these plans match your financial status and future objectives, enabling you to make well-informed decisions about properties.

[HEADING-H2] The legal and ethical implications of group boycotting in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] Group boycotting in the real estate industry has become an increasingly controversial topic. While some argue it helps level the playing field, others see it as unethical and potentially illegal. This article examines the complex issues surrounding group boycotting and why it often crosses legal and ethical lines.
[HEADING-H2] What is group boycotting?
[PARAGRAPH] Group boycotting refers to when multiple real estate brokers or agents collectively agree to not work with or share commissions with certain other brokers or agents. For example, a group of agents may decide to never show houses listed by a particular brokerage or never refer clients to a specific agent. The goal is to freeze out and weaken the business of targeted individuals or companies.
[PARAGRAPH] On the surface, group boycotting may seem like fair competition. If agents don’t want to work with someone, that should be their choice, right? But in reality, group boycotting often violates antitrust laws and ethical business practices for several key reasons.
[HEADING-H3] Restraint of trade
[PARAGRAPH] Group boycotting essentially amounts to collusion among competitors. When agents collectively agree not to work with a broker or agent, they are restraining trade and reducing competition in the marketplace. This violates antitrust laws, such as the Sherman Antitrust Act, which prohibits anticompetitive agreements.
[HEADING-H3] Access denied
[PARAGRAPH] Group boycotting often cuts off access to an essential service that certain brokers or agents need to properly conduct business. Limiting access to the MLS database or refusing to show certain listed properties makes it very difficult for targeted individuals to fully participate in the market.
[HEADING-H3] Client steering
[PARAGRAPH] Boycotting groups will frequently steer clients away from doing business with the agent or brokerage they are targeting. This interferes with the client’s ability to freely choose who they want to work with. Client steering based on a group boycott rather than the client’s best interests is unethical.
[HEADING-H3] Divisiveness
[PARAGRAPH] Group boycotting breeds divisiveness and toxicity within the real estate community. It creates an “us vs. them” mentality that damages professional cooperation and problem-solving. This toxic environment ultimately hurts consumers.
[PARAGRAPH] While competition breeds excellence, group boycotting tends to breed dysfunction. There are more ethical ways for real estate professionals to further their interests without resorting to potentially illegal and unprofessional tactics. Change is better accomplished through constructive action, not punitive boycotting.

[HEADING-H2] What is a Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS) is applicable to properties in the construction process, commonly referred to as Buildings Under Construction (BUC).
[PARAGRAPH] As its name implies, PSS allows homebuyers to increase payments as the development progresses. This typically ranges from 5 to 10% of the property purchase price at specific milestones during construction. In the case of resale condos, a 25% down payment is required, and monthly repayments begin immediately.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, you would make an instalment to the developer upon completion of the foundation, another payment when the walls are erected, and a further one when the roofs are prepared.
[PARAGRAPH] The benefit of this scheme is that it offers lower initial monthly repayments, and even if delays in the developer’s timeline or milestones are not met, the loan repayments remain unchanged.
[HEADING-H2] How does a Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS) work?
[PARAGRAPH] The process works in such a way that once a particular stage of the construction is finished, the developers will inform your lawyer through a notice about the required progress payment for that stage.
[PARAGRAPH] Depending on your financing agreement, you must either pay in cash, or the bank providing the loan will be notified to release a disbursement.
[PARAGRAPH] The payment must be made to the developer within 14 days of receiving the notice, as failure to do so will result in the application of late payment charges.
[HEADING-H2] What are the stages in the Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS)?
[PARAGRAPH] The following are the stages of construction for a property under the BUC loan, along with the corresponding percentage of the purchase price that is typically disbursed at each stage:
[LIST-ITEM] Foundation work: 10%
[LIST-ITEM] Reinforced concrete work: 10%
[LIST-ITEM] Partition walls: 5%
[LIST-ITEM] Roofing: 5%
[LIST-ITEM] Door sub-frames, window frames, electrical wiring, internal plastering, and plumbing: 5%
[LIST-ITEM] Car parks, roads, and drains serving the housing project: 5%
[LIST-ITEM] Building, roads, drainage, sewage works, and the connection of utilities: This stage marks a significant milestone as the Temporary Occupation Permit (TOP) is typically released. At this stage, 25% of the purchase price is disbursed to cover the remaining construction works.
[PARAGRAPH] Buyers can collect their keys and move into the property after obtaining the TOP.
[LIST-ITEM] Final Payment Date and/or Completion: The final stage involves the remaining 15% of the purchase price being disbursed, which may be further staggered depending on when the Certificate of Statutory Completion (CSC) is issued.
[PARAGRAPH] The CSC signifies the completion of all construction works and grants full legal status to the property.
[HEADING-H2] What should I know about the Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS)?
[PARAGRAPH] Builders may issue a notice of completion for multiple construction phases simultaneously, requiring buyers to make several stage payments simultaneously. This typically occurs when purchasing a property from another buyer at a later stage, after the initial launch. In such cases, buyers may be expected to fulfil several progressive payment stages together after signing the Sales and Purchase Agreement (S&PA).
[PARAGRAPH] It is important to note that the payment process can vary across different new launch condo projects. Therefore, buyers should be aware that the specific payment terms and arrangements may differ for each project.

[HEADING-H2] What is a break-even price?
[PARAGRAPH] The break-even price refers to the point at which a transaction or investment yields neither profit nor loss. It represents the price at which the revenue generated from selling a product or asset covers all the costs associated with its acquisition, ownership, or production.
[PARAGRAPH] Break-even prices are applicable across various scenarios and transactions. For instance, in the context of property ownership, the break-even price would be the selling price that allows the owner to recover all expenses related to the property. This includes the purchase price, mortgage interest, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, improvements, closing costs, and real estate sales commissions. The homeowner would not generate a profit or incur losses at this price.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, consider an individual who invests S$750,000 in purchasing and maintaining a house. They would reach the break-even point by selling the property for the same amount. Alternatively, if they rent the house for S$2,500 per month, it would take approximately 300 months to reach the break-even point.
[PARAGRAPH] Break-even prices also apply if the individual decides to develop the land and construct the house independently. In such cases, the break-even price would represent the amount that covers the costs of land acquisition, construction materials, labour, permits, and other associated expenses.
[HEADING-H2] How to calculate break-even prices for real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] To calculate the break-even point for real estate, you must determine the specific selling price or rental income required to cover all the expenses associated with acquiring, owning, or developing the property. It is important to note that the break-even formula serves as a guideline, and individual circumstances and factors can influence the accuracy and applicability of the calculated break-even price.
[PARAGRAPH] The break-even selling price formula for real estate is as follows:
[PARAGRAPH] Break-even Selling Price = Purchase price + Mortgage interest + Insurance + Property taxes (e.g., Seller’s Stamp Duty) + Maintenance costs + Improvements + Closing costs + Real estate sales commissions

[HEADING-H2] What is a cul-de-sac house?
[PARAGRAPH] A cul-de-sac is a street typically characterised by a semicircular road at a closed end. Unlike other streets that meet at right angles to form corners, cul-de-sacs do not have any corners.
[PARAGRAPH] Cul-de-sac houses are properties located on these streets. Despite its French name, which means “bottom of the sack,” cul-de-sacs create an attractive residential neighbourhood.
[PARAGRAPH] While it is similar to a dead-end street, a cul-de-sac offers a more aesthetically pleasing exit. Rather than having to awkwardly back down the street or turn around in someone’s driveway like on a dead-end street, you can simply drive around the semicircular road and return to where you started.
[HEADING-H2] What are the advantages and disadvantages of a cul-de-sac house?
[HEADING-H2] Advantages
[PARAGRAPH] Cul-de-sacs are a popular choice for many people because there is minimal traffic on the road. This can create a sense of safety and security as any suspicious activity will likely be noticed quickly due to the low traffic volume.
[PARAGRAPH] With fewer cars on the road, safety is heightened as drivers tend to drive at slower speeds due to the proximity of their destination. This makes it safer for children to play outside and ride their bikes without worry.
[PARAGRAPH] Additionally, pet owners can feel more at ease as there are fewer potential hazards for their pets to encounter on the cul-de-sac.
[PARAGRAPH] Living in a cul-de-sac often means that houses face each other in a semi-circle or are closer together, promoting stronger relationships among neighbours. Residents have more opportunities to interact, which can lead to getting to know each other better.
[PARAGRAPH] This increased closeness also helps prevent crime, as neighbours can watch each other’s properties and children, reducing the risk of incidents such as burglary, vandalism, or fire.
[PARAGRAPH] Children also benefit by having playmates nearby, which can help foster a strong sense of community. Those who enjoy being part of a close-knit neighbourhood would likely appreciate the sense of community that comes with living on a cul-de-sac.
[HEADING-H2] Disadvantages
[PARAGRAPH] The size of a cul-de-sac may impact the amount of available parking, which can be limited compared to a standard street.
[PARAGRAPH] This could become a problem if a neighbour hosts a party with many guests, potentially occupying all available parking spots and blocking a neighbour’s walkway.
[PARAGRAPH] If many people leave for work simultaneously in the morning, it could cause traffic problems.
[PARAGRAPH] Besides, having just one entry and exit point in the neighbourhood can cause delays during emergencies or lead to traffic congestion. This means it may take longer to reach your destination in such situations.
[PARAGRAPH] Privacy can be a concern when residing in a cul-de-sac, especially if it is important to you.
[PARAGRAPH] Due to the proximity of homes, neighbours are typically nearby, and finding a completely secluded area can be difficult.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) is Singapore’s primary land-use planning and conservation authority. Established in 1974, its origins can be traced back to the Urban Renewal Department, created by the Housing and Development Board (HDB) in the 1960s.
[PARAGRAPH] Guided by its mission to create an appealing city for residents, workers, and leisure seekers alike, the URA plays a vital role in meticulously planning and facilitating the physical development of Singapore.
[PARAGRAPH] What does the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) do?
[PARAGRAPH] Initially focused on land sales and urban renewal in the Central Area, the URA now has a wide range of responsibilities, including the following:
[PARAGRAPH] The Concept Plan is reviewed every 10 years and translated into a Master Plan, a statutory guide for development over 10-15 years. The Master Plan provides specific land use and density details and is reviewed every five years.
[PARAGRAPH] Based on the plans outlined in the Concept Plan and Master Plan, land is allocated for development.
[PARAGRAPH] These controls safeguard the broader community’s interests while allowing property owners and businesses to develop their holdings.
[PARAGRAPH] This programme offers opportunities for development and investment.
[PARAGRAPH] Guidelines and principles are established to ensure the high-quality restoration of these structures, involving collaboration with owners, architects, engineers, and contractors.
[PARAGRAPH] When envisioning the city centre, they carefully consider the relationship between buildings and streets, how people interact with them, and the overall urban experience.
[PARAGRAPH] Managing public parking lots in the Central Area, commercial and industrial areas outside HDB estates, and certain private residential estates are also part of their responsibilities.

[HEADING-H2] What is HVAC?
[PARAGRAPH] HVAC stands for Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning. It’s a system used to provide thermal comfort and acceptable indoor air quality. In Singapore’s real estate market, HVAC systems are an important feature in both residential and commercial properties.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding HVAC
[PARAGRAPH] HVAC systems control the temperature, humidity, and air quality in buildings. They involve a range of components including heating and cooling units, ventilation ducts, and controls that manage the system. HVAC systems can vary in complexity, from simple window air conditioners to complex central heating and cooling systems.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of HVAC in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] In the context of Singapore’s real estate market, HVAC systems are crucial for maintaining a comfortable and healthy indoor environment. For residential properties, a well-functioning HVAC system can contribute to a home’s comfort and energy efficiency.
[PARAGRAPH] For commercial properties, a well-functioning HVAC system can contribute to higher productivity and better health for employees. In addition, the quality and efficiency of a property’s HVAC system can affect its value and appeal to potential buyers or tenants.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] HVAC systems play a crucial role in real estate, contributing to the comfort and health of building occupants. Understanding these systems can help property owners and managers maintain their properties more effectively. However, installing and maintaining HVAC systems can be complex and costly, and it’s often advisable to seek professional advice.

[HEADING-H3] Definition of amendments
[PARAGRAPH] A (property) amendment is a formal or official modification made to a real estate contract, lease agreement, or any other property-related legal document in Singapore. In the realm of Singaporean real estate, such amendments are frequently employed to alter the terms of a property purchase contract or lease agreement.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding amendments
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore’s property market, amendments can be utilised to modify various aspects of a real estate contract, such as the purchase price, completion date, or other terms of the agreement. These amendments offer a level of flexibility, allowing all parties involved to adapt the agreement based on changes in circumstances or negotiations.
[PARAGRAPH] The process of amending a document in Singapore depends on the nature of the document. For instance, in the context of Singapore’s property market, amending a lease agreement for a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat often requires a higher level of agreement, such as the consent of all parties involved, compared to other types of property agreements. This is to ensure that such significant changes reflect a broad consensus among the stakeholders, rather than the preferences of a single party.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of amendments in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] Property amendments serve as a means of modifying existing agreements or laws without entirely discarding them. They allow for flexibility and adaptation over time, which is vital in a rapidly evolving city-state like Singapore, where social, economic, and technological changes are constantly taking place. Property amendments can be instrumental in maintaining current legal standards and ensuring the fairness and relevance of laws and regulations in the real estate sector.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Property amendments play a pivotal role in Singapore’s real estate contracts, offering the necessary flexibility to adapt to changing circumstances. Understanding how to effectively use property amendments can assist parties in navigating negotiations and reaching satisfactory agreements. These amendments are often integrated into the relevant sections of the original document.
[PARAGRAPH] If they’re extensive, it may be more practical to rewrite the document incorporating the changes entirely. Property amendments can be instrumental in maintaining current legal standards and ensuring the fairness and relevance of laws and regulations in Singapore’s real estate sector.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the Government Land Sales (GLS) programme?
[PARAGRAPH] The Government Land Sales (GLS) Programme is essential to implementing Singapore’s Long-Term and Master Plans. Its purpose is to release state land for development, driving the planned growth and improving the country’s physical environment.
[PARAGRAPH] The GLS Programme operates biannually, announcing available land parcels categorised into the Confirmed and Reserve lists.
[PARAGRAPH] How does the Government Land Sales (GLS) programme work?
[PARAGRAPH] Before the start of each half-year, the government releases State Land for tender through the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) sites.
[PARAGRAPH] Interested developers who wish to acquire the State Land for residential development, such as constructing new condominiums, participate in an open tender process where they bid for the land. Generally, the developer submitting the highest bid in the open tender will be awarded the land.
[PARAGRAPH] Once the tender period concludes, URA issues a media statement disclosing the awarded GLS sites and the respective developers. Subsequently, another media statement will be released to inform the public about the list of developers who tendered for the site and the quoted prices in their tenders.
[PARAGRAPH] The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, head over to the official websites.

[HEADING-H2] Land theft through fear: The devastating reality of intimidation tactics in land grabbing
[PARAGRAPH] Land grabbing refers to illegally or fraudulently acquiring land that a person or party is not legally entitled to. This often involves intimidation tactics such as threats or the use of force to compel the legal owner to give up their land. Though land disputes are not uncommon, especially in developing countries, the practice of land grabbing through intimidation is illegal, unethical, and causes great distress.
[PARAGRAPH] One common tactic is when an individual or business coerces farmers into handing over the land title through deception, manipulation, or outright threats. They may take advantage of poor, uneducated farmers who lack the resources to defend their rights. Violence is also used in some cases, where armed gangs force people off their ancestrally owned land. Some common methods of illegal land grabbing through intimidation include:
[LIST-ITEM] Making false claims to the land with forged title deeds or other fraudulent documents. This is common when land records are poorly maintained.
[LIST-ITEM] Threatening violence or retaliation against the landowner and their family if they do not comply with demands to give up the land. This can involve verbal threats or physical assault.
[LIST-ITEM] Destroying or damaging property, livestock, crops, or homes is an act of intimidation. The aim is to make continued ownership practically impossible.
[LIST-ITEM] Bribing local officials to turn a blind eye or actively assist with the illegal land seizure.
[LIST-ITEM] Taking advantage of political instability, weak governance, and lack of legal protections in certain regions.
[PARAGRAPH] Land grabbing affects vulnerable groups worldwide, especially rural farmers in developing nations. However, it violates basic human rights and causes emotional trauma in addition to financial loss. Intimidation is an unscrupulous method to acquire land illegally at the expense of others.
[PARAGRAPH] Governments must strengthen property laws, improve land record-keeping, and prosecute land grabbers to protect owner rights. Victims should also unite with local and international advocacy groups working against land grabbing. With vigilance and a stand for human rights, communities can counter intimidation and uphold justice.

[HEADING-H2] What are serviced apartments?
[PARAGRAPH] Serviced apartments, also known as service apartments or SAs, are fully furnished apartments that offer a seamless blend of home comforts and hotel-like facilities. These apartments cater to a diverse range of residents, including expatriates, business travellers, families, and tourists.
[PARAGRAPH] Featuring complete furnishings and essential appliances, serviced apartments provide the convenience of kitchenettes or full kitchens. Alongside these amenities, residents can enjoy various support services such as concierge assistance, common dining areas, housekeeping, and laundry facilities.
[PARAGRAPH] Location plays a vital role in the appeal of serviced apartments. They are often strategically positioned in sought-after neighbourhoods close to business districts, shopping centres, dining options, and transportation hubs. This proximity grants residents easy access to amenities, services, and public transportation, enhancing convenience and facilitating the exploration of the city and its surroundings.
[PARAGRAPH] Serviced apartments typically require a minimum stay of seven days or longer. Residents also have the option to choose longer stays, accommodating various needs, whether it’s a short business trip, temporary relocation, or an extended stay.
[PARAGRAPH] Renting a serviced apartment offers a luxurious living experience at a more affordable price compared to staying in a hotel. Furthermore, individuals planning to stay for an extended period can benefit from tax savings.
[HEADING-H2] What is the cost of serviced apartments?
[PARAGRAPH] Generally, serviced apartments are priced higher than traditional rental apartments due to their added convenience and services, reflecting the additional convenience and services they offer.
[PARAGRAPH] The cost of serviced apartments in Singapore varies depending on location, size, facilities, and duration of stay, ranging from S$1,000 to S$10,000.
[HEADING-H2] Are serviced apartments legal in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] The legality of serviced apartments in Singapore is governed by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) guidelines. These guidelines allow serviced apartments in certain areas, including residential zones and mixed-use sites where residential use is permitted.
[PARAGRAPH] However, strata subdivision of serviced apartments is strictly prohibited. This means serviced apartments must be developed and managed under a single ownership structure.
[HEADING-H2] Is a serviced apartment a good investment?
[PARAGRAPH] Investing in serviced apartments can offer several advantages. Firstly, the demand for serviced apartments in Singapore is driven by factors such as business travel, relocation, and tourism. The city-state attracts many expatriates, corporate travellers, and tourists seeking the convenience and comfort of serviced apartments. This consistent demand can translate into higher occupancy rates and investor rental yields.
[PARAGRAPH] Additionally, serviced apartments can offer greater flexibility compared to traditional rental properties. Depending on market conditions and personal preferences, investors can choose to rent out their units for short-term or long-term stays. This flexibility increases rental rates during peak periods, such as major events or holiday seasons.
[PARAGRAPH] Moreover, serviced apartments are typically managed by professional operators who handle property maintenance, guest services, and marketing. This can relieve investors of the day-to-day management responsibilities and ensure a hassle-free investment experience.
[PARAGRAPH] However, it’s important for investors to carefully evaluate the potential risks and challenges associated with serviced apartments. Market fluctuations, changes in regulations, and competition from other accommodation options can impact the profitability of the investment. Conducting thorough market research, understanding the target tenant profile, and working with reputable operators are essential steps to mitigate these risks.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the Offer to Purchase?
[PARAGRAPH] How does the Offer to Purchase work?
[PARAGRAPH] The Offer to Purchase, typically prepared by the buyer’s representative, is accompanied by a check amounting to approximately 1% of the purchase price. This check is a deposit intended for use in the OTP.
[PARAGRAPH] Once the seller agrees to the terms, they sign the Offer to Purchase and may proceed to issue the OTP to the buyer.
[PARAGRAPH] In the event that the seller decides to reject the Offer to Purchase or if the validity period of the Offer expires without an OTP being issued, it becomes the seller’s responsibility to return the check to the buyer.
[PARAGRAPH] Hence, the seller mustn’t deposit the buyer’s check before signing the Offer. This precaution is necessary to avoid inadvertently transforming the Offer into a legally binding contract, similar to the OTP.
[PARAGRAPH] What is in the Offer to Purchase?
[PARAGRAPH] The Offer to Purchase includes the following essential details:
[LIST-ITEM] Property address
[LIST-ITEM] Proposed price for the property
[LIST-ITEM] Duration of the OTP, which is typically 14 days, although it is possible to request a longer duration
[LIST-ITEM] Specified date for completing the transaction, usually around 6 weeks after exercising the option, with the flexibility to request additional time if needed
[LIST-ITEM] Validity period of the Offer to Purchase, typically lasting for 3 days
[LIST-ITEM] Additional terms that should be incorporated into the Option to Purchase, such as a 5% deposit
[LIST-ITEM] Inclusion of the “subject to contract” clause in the heading
[PARAGRAPH] Do I need an Offer to Purchase if I already have an Option to Purchase (OTP)?
[PARAGRAPH] While it is possible for buyers and sellers to proceed directly to the OTP without sending an Offer to Purchase initially, property agents widely follow the practice of sending an Offer letter.
[PARAGRAPH] The Offer to Purchase lets buyers specify the terms in the subsequent OTP. For example, if you upgrade from an HDB flat to a condominium and depend on the cash proceeds from selling your flat, requesting a longer OTP period can provide you with more time to carefully evaluate and accept the best Offer for your flat.
[PARAGRAPH] Likewise, the offer letter can indicate the desired completion date, which is vital for buyers to know when the transaction will be concluded, enabling them to plan their move-in accordingly.
[PARAGRAPH] Therefore, if you have decided to make an offer for a resale property, it is recommended to engage the services of an agent to professionally draft a formal Offer to Purchase.

[HEADING-H2] What is proration?
[PARAGRAPH] Proration is the division of certain costs between the buyer and seller at the closing of a real estate transaction. In Singapore’s real estate market, proration can be used to divide costs such as property taxes or utility bills.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding proration:
[PARAGRAPH] Proration involves dividing ongoing expenses or income between the buyer and seller based on the closing date of the transaction. For instance, if a property is sold in the middle of a month, the seller might be responsible for half of that month’s property taxes, with the buyer responsible for the other half.
[PARAGRAPH] Proration can apply to various types of expenses or income, including property taxes, homeowners association fees, rent, or utility bills.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of proration in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] In the context of real estate transactions, proration ensures that the buyer and seller each pay their fair share of ongoing expenses or income. It’s a common practice in real estate transactions and is usually negotiated as part of the closing process.
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore, proration can be particularly important in transactions involving rental properties, where the rent and other ongoing expenses need to be divided between the buyer and seller.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Proration is a crucial part of real estate transactions, ensuring that ongoing expenses or income are fairly divided between the buyer and seller. Understanding this process can help buyers and sellers navigate their transactions more effectively. However, proration can be a complex process, and it’s often advisable to seek the assistance of a real estate professional or attorney.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the HDB Fiance/Fiancee Scheme?
[PARAGRAPH] The Fiancé/Fiancée Scheme allows couples to purchase an HDB flat together as a family unit before officially marrying.

[HEADING-H2] The art of the deal: How mediation helps opposing parties find common ground
[PARAGRAPH] In any negotiation or dispute, parties often become entrenched in their positions and fail to see potential areas for compromise. Emotions run high, communication breaks down, and progress stalls. However, with the help of an impartial mediator, even the most contentious disagreements can move toward resolution. Mediation provides a structured process for opponents to find common ground.
[HEADING-H3] The mediator’s role
[PARAGRAPH] Unlike a judge or arbitrator who decides the outcome, a mediator facilitates communication and guides the parties themselves to a mutually agreeable settlement. The mediator creates a safe space for open dialogue, ensuring all voices are heard. They identify key issues, interests, and needs on each side. By translating anger into understanding, a skilled mediator transforms conflict into cooperation.
[PARAGRAPH] The mediator asks probing questions to uncover why the dispute arose and what is truly at stake. Oftentimes, beneath the surface arguments lie deeper motivations – the real roots of discord. For example, noise complaints between neighbours may stem from a need for security, not just annoyance. The mediator helps reframe positions into interests to find win-win solutions.
[HEADING-H3] Moving from positions to interests
[PARAGRAPH] Rather than locking into rigid stances, mediation encourages flexibility. Parties shift focus from hardened positions to the underlying interests, needs, and concerns that drive them. New options emerge as shared goals are uncovered. A business dispute over contract terms may reveal mutual interests in profitability and continued partnership. Suddenly, collaborative problem-solving becomes possible.
[PARAGRAPH] Parties also begin to understand the legitimacy of the other side’s perspective. Empathy develops, tensions ease, and creative problem-solving expands. Vision broadens from narrow self-interest to the bigger picture and collective good.
[HEADING-H3] The win-win mindset
[PARAGRAPH] Ultimately, mediation is about finding win-win solutions that work for all involved. When parties reach a mutual understanding and satisfy core interests, durable agreements result. Mediation transforms the mindset from adversarial to cooperative, from zero-sum to positive sum. With an expert mediator’s guidance, skilful negotiation turns conflict into an opportunity for gain rather than loss. Even bitter foes can find common ground with the art of the deal that mediation facilitates.
[PARAGRAPH] Mediation provides a path beyond impasse for opposing parties. Through facilitated dialogue, shared interests are uncovered, innovative solutions emerge, and mutually beneficial settlements are reached. With patience and an open mind, the art of negotiation can lead to breakthroughs where all sides feel heard, respected, and satisfied.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Home Protection Scheme (HPS)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is an insurance that reduces mortgages. The scheme aims to safeguard HDB owners from unforeseen circumstances that could hinder them from repaying their housing loans.
[PARAGRAPH] Administered by the Central Provident Fund Board (CPFB), HPS provides claim eligibility to your family if you pass away, get diagnosed with a terminal illness, or become permanently disabled. The claim amount from HPS is the remaining balance of your HDB home loan.
[PARAGRAPH] In other words, if you pass away with S$50,000 still owed in your housing loan, HPS will cover the entire amount, relieving your family of the repayment burden.
[PARAGRAPH] HPS is comparable to mortgage insurance policies offered by some insurance companies. If you purchase an HDB flat with HPS coverage, there is no need to buy a separate insurance policy. It’s also worth noting that HPS is significantly less expensive than other private mortgage insurance.
[HEADING-H2] How long does coverage under the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) last?
[PARAGRAPH] HPS members are covered until they reach age 65 or until their mortgages are paid off, whichever comes first.
[HEADING-H2] How to be eligible for the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) coverage?
[PARAGRAPH] To be eligible for HPS coverage, you need to be in good health.
[PARAGRAPH] You are not eligible for HPS if you have major pre-existing medical conditions such as kidney failure, cancer, liver failure or transplant, or diabetes with complications like retinopathy or nephropathy. However, you can still use your CPF funds to repay your mortgage.
[PARAGRAPH] Rather than having a comprehensive list of pre-existing conditions, the CPF Board reviews each case based on the severity, prognosis, and management of the medical condition and the applicant’s health risk profile.
[HEADING-H2] What kinds of conditions are not covered by HPS claims?
[PARAGRAPH] HPS, like other insurance policies, has certain exclusions that prevent claims from being made during the first year of coverage if death or permanent incapacitation is caused by self-harm, suicide, a criminal offence carrying a death sentence, or an intentional criminal act.
[PARAGRAPH] Claims also cannot be made under HPS if any of the information provided during the application was incorrect or deceptive or if the claim stemmed from participation in a conflict or riot.
[HEADING-H2] Is the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) mandatory?
[PARAGRAPH] The Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board mandates the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) for Singaporeans who use CPF to partially or fully pay for their monthly home loan payments unless they have an exemption or pre-existing condition that disqualifies them.
[PARAGRAPH] However, if you are not utilising CPF funds to pay for your home loan, you can still opt for coverage under HPS. HPS exclusively applies to HDB or DBSS flats, but not to private residences such as condominiums, executive condominiums (ECs), HUDC flats, and landed properties. Furthermore, HPS only applies if you have a housing loan.
[HEADING-H2] What are Home Protection Scheme (HPS) exemptions?
[PARAGRAPH] You can only be exempt from the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) if your personal insurance plans fully cover the remaining loan amount for your HDB flat in case of death, terminal illness, or permanent disability. This coverage should last until your loan ends or until you turn 65, whichever happens first.
[PARAGRAPH] You can use the following types of insurance policies, either traditional or investment-linked, to back your application for exemption:
[LIST-ITEM] Whole Life
[LIST-ITEM] Term Life
[LIST-ITEM] Endowments
[LIST-ITEM] Life Riders (must be attached to a basic policy)
[LIST-ITEM] Mortgage Reducing Term Assurance (MRTA)/Decreasing Term Rider
[HEADING-H2] How much is the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) Premium?
[PARAGRAPH] HPS premiums are determined based on five factors;
[LIST-ITEM] The outstanding housing loan
[LIST-ITEM] Loan repayment period
[LIST-ITEM] Type of loan (concessionary or market rate)
[LIST-ITEM] Age and gender of the member
[LIST-ITEM] And the percentage share of cover for the flat.
[PARAGRAPH] You must only pay premiums for 90% of your HPS coverage period. It means that if you need coverage for 25 years, you will only have to pay premiums for the first 22.5 years. The remaining 2.5 years of coverage will not require any premium payments.
[HEADING-H2] How to pay for the Home Protection Scheme (HPS)?
[PARAGRAPH] You can pay your HPS premiums using your CPF Ordinary Account (OA) funds. The amount is automatically deducted on an annual basis.
[PARAGRAPH] If your OA does not have enough funds, you must make a cash payment to avoid any impact on your HPS coverage. Alternatively, your co-owner can authorise CPF to deduct premiums from their CPF account to pay for your HPS coverage.

[PARAGRAPH] Who really owns your home? The need-to-know basics of vesting in real estate
How property ownership is vested – meaning who actually owns the title to real estate – is an important consideration for homebuyers. Understanding the basics of vesting can help ensure your property rights are properly protected.
[HEADING-H2] What is vesting?
[PARAGRAPH] Vesting refers to how ownership of real estate is held. When you purchase a home, the deed and title to the property must be vested, or granted, to the owner or owners. There are several common ways homes can be vested:
[LIST-ITEM] Sole ownership: The home is titled and deeded only to one individual. This is the simplest form of vesting.
[LIST-ITEM] Joint tenancy: Joint tenancy establishes equal ownership interest between two or more people. If one owner dies, their share automatically goes to the surviving owner(s). This avoids probate.
[LIST-ITEM] Tenancy in common: Like joint tenancy, tenancy in common involves shared ownership between two or more people. However, each owner holds a separate share that can be willed to another person upon death.
[LIST-ITEM] Community property: In some states, property acquired during a marriage is considered jointly owned by both spouses. Each spouse has an undivided equal interest.
[LIST-ITEM] Trusts: Property can be titled and ownership vested into a living trust. This allows a designated person to manage the property on behalf of the beneficiaries.
[HEADING-H3] Choosing the right vesting
[PARAGRAPH] When purchasing a home, it’s important to consider how you want the property vested. This decision should be made carefully with your plans for the home in mind.
[PARAGRAPH] If you purchase with a spouse or partner, joint tenancy with the right of survivorship ensures your partner will inherit your share. For unrelated co-buyers, tenancy in common allows more flexibility.
[PARAGRAPH] Trusts can be useful for estate planning purposes. Consult with a real estate attorney to decide the optimal vesting method for your situation.
[PARAGRAPH] Vesting protects your rights and outlines exactly who owns the property. Be sure to understand this legal component before buying or selling real estate. With the right vesting approach, you can avoid complications down the road.
