[HEADING-H2] What is PSI?
[PARAGRAPH] PSI, or Pollutant Standards Index, is a measure of air quality. In Singapore, PSI levels can have an impact on real estate, affecting both residential and commercial properties.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding PSI
[PARAGRAPH] The PSI is a number used by governments to inform the public about the level of air pollution. It can range from 0 to 500, with higher numbers indicating worse air quality. The PSI takes into account several pollutants, including particulate matter, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of PSI in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] In the context of Singapore’s real estate market, high PSI levels can affect property values and rental rates. For instance, properties in areas with consistently high PSI levels might be less desirable, leading to lower property values or rental rates.
[PARAGRAPH] On the other hand, properties with features that can mitigate the effects of poor air quality, such as advanced HVAC systems or indoor air purifiers, might be more desirable in areas with high PSI levels.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] PSI levels can have an impact on real estate in Singapore, affecting property values and rental rates. Understanding this can help property owners, investors, and tenants make informed decisions. However, dealing with high PSI levels can be challenging, and it’s often advisable to seek professional advice on how to mitigate the effects of poor air quality.

[HEADING-H2] The power of bonds: How they secure real estate deals and protect your investment
[PARAGRAPH] Real estate deals can be risky business. The process of buying, selling, or developing property often requires large investments upfront, with the hope of profits down the road. However, unforeseen circumstances can derail a real estate project, leaving investors exposed. This is where the power of bonds comes in.
[HEADING-H3] What is a bond?
[PARAGRAPH] A bond is a financial instrument that provides a form of insurance on a real estate project. The three main types of bonds used in real estate are:
[LIST-ITEM] Bid bonds – A guarantee a contractor will follow through on their bid for a project.
[LIST-ITEM] Performance bonds – A guarantee a contractor will complete the project as specified in the contract.
[LIST-ITEM] Payment Bonds – Guarantee subcontractors and suppliers will be paid for their work.
[LIST-ITEM] The party purchasing the bond pays a premium to the surety company issuing the bond. If the bonded party fails to uphold their end of the deal, the surety company pays the damages up to the bond amount to make the injured party whole.
[HEADING-H3] Securing the deal
[PARAGRAPH] For real estate investors, requiring bonding from contractors is a prudent way to secure deals and mitigate risks. Bid bonds weed out contractors who cannot complete a project. Performance and payment bonds provide assurance contractors will perform the work properly and pay their subcontractors. This transfers risk away from the investor.
[PARAGRAPH] Without these bonds, investors take on substantial risks in hiring contractors. Shoddy workmanship, cost overruns, and abandoned projects can quickly turn profits into losses. Requiring bonding aligns incentives and ensures contractors have skin in the game.
[HEADING-H3] Protecting your investment
[PARAGRAPH] Bonding also plays a vital role in protecting investments if problems do arise. For example, if a contractor fails to complete a project, the surety company behind the performance bond will step in to find a new contractor or provide financial compensation. This protects the investor’s capital outlay.
[PARAGRAPH] Likewise, payment bonds give subcontractors and suppliers recourse if the general contractor fails to pay. The surety company satisfies these obligations, preventing liens on the property that could inhibit sale or occupancy. This preserves the asset’s value.
[PARAGRAPH] Bonds provide a crucial backstop for real estate investors, limiting financial risk and preventing deals from going sideways. Given the large sums often involved, paying bond premiums is inexpensive and worthwhile insurance.
[PARAGRAPH] While bonding does not eliminate all real estate risks, its ability to transfer and mitigate key perils makes it an indispensable tool for securing transactions and protecting investments. The power of bonds brings peace of mind to even the most complex deal.

[HEADING-H2] What is covenant?
[PARAGRAPH] A covenant is a promise in a written contract or deed of real property. In Singapore’s real estate market, covenants are often used to enforce certain restrictions or obligations.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding covenant
[PARAGRAPH] A covenant in real estate is a promise that a buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord makes regarding the use or maintenance of a property. Covenants can be “positive,” requiring the party to perform certain actions, or “restrictive,” prohibiting the party from certain actions. Covenants are legally binding and can be enforced through legal action if one party fails to fulfil their obligations.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of covenant in real estate and property
[PARAGRAPH] In the context of real estate, covenants can be used to enforce certain restrictions or obligations. For instance, a covenant might restrict a homeowner from making certain changes to their property in order to maintain the aesthetic of a neighbourhood.
[PARAGRAPH] Covenants can also be used to enforce maintenance obligations, such as a requirement for a homeowner to maintain their property in a certain condition. In Singapore, covenants are often used in lease agreements, where the tenant agrees to certain terms such as paying rent on time or maintaining the property. They can also be used in property sales contracts, where the buyer and seller agree to certain terms regarding the sale and use of the property.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Covenants play a crucial role in real estate, helping to enforce certain restrictions or obligations. Understanding how covenants work can help property owners, buyers, and tenants navigate their contractual obligations more effectively.
[PARAGRAPH] Nevertheless, because covenants are legal obligations, it’s often advisable to seek legal advice when entering into a covenant.

[HEADING-H2] What is equalisation?
[PARAGRAPH] Equalisation rates play a pivotal role in real estate by ensuring fairness and consistency in property valuation.
[PARAGRAPH] These rates, also known as assessment ratios or assessment levels, are integral to the property tax system and are used to align property values with market realities.
[PARAGRAPH] Simply put, equalisation rates are calculated to balance assessed property values with their fair market values.
[HEADING-H2] How do equalisation rates work?
[PARAGRAPH] They are expressed as a ratio or percentage and reflect the relationship between the assessed value of a property and its actual market value. In a perfect scenario, the equalisation rate would be 100%, indicating that the assessed and market values are identical.
[PARAGRAPH] However, due to the dynamic nature of real estate markets, assessed values may lag behind or exceed market values. This is where equalisation rates come into play. If an area’s real estate market is experiencing rapid appreciation, property assessments might not keep up with the escalating values. Conversely, assessments could remain higher than the current market conditions warrant in a declining market.
[PARAGRAPH] Assessors and tax authorities adjust property values using equalisation rates to rectify these discrepancies. For instance, if the equalisation rate is below 100%, it implies that the assessed values need to be increased to align with the market. Conversely, an equalisation rate above 100% signals that assessed values should be reduced to match the market. This process helps ensure that property owners are taxed fairly based on their property’s true value.
[HEADING-H2] How to calculate equalisation rates?
[PARAGRAPH] If we have an equalisation rate of 0.80, it means that the value assigned to a property for tax purposes is 80% of its total worth. Let’s imagine there’s a property that’s evaluated to be worth S$100,000, and the equalisation rate is 0.80.
[PARAGRAPH] To figure out the whole value, the formula employed is: Full Value = Assessed Value divided by Equalisation Rate.
[PARAGRAPH] This calculation yields a Full Value of S$125,000.
[HEADING-H2] What factors influence equalisation rates?
[PARAGRAPH] Several factors influence the determination of equalisation rates, including:
[LIST-ITEM] Real estate market trends: The primary driver is the state of the local real estate market. If property values are rapidly increasing or declining, it affects the relationship between assessed values and market values.
[LIST-ITEM] Data collection and analysis: Accurate assessment requires reliable data on property sales, local economic conditions, and market trends. Effective data collection and analysis methodologies contribute to more precise equalisation rates.
[LIST-ITEM] Property types: Different property types, such as residential, commercial, and industrial, might experience varying market trends, affecting the overall equalisation rate.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) is a housing grant provided through CPF, specifically designed for first-time flat buyers who are either applying for a new Build-To-Order (BTO) flat or purchasing a resale flat in the open market.
[PARAGRAPH] Its main purpose is to improve housing affordability and make housing more accessible to Singaporeans.
[HEADING-H2] Am I eligible for the Enhanced Housing Grant?
[PARAGRAPH] To qualify for the EHG, you must
[PARAGRAPH] meet the following requirements:
[LIST-ITEM] You must be a first-time applicant for a flat.
[LIST-ITEM] Your average gross monthly household income for the previous 12 months must be below S$9,000.
[LIST-ITEM] You must have been continuously employed for the past 12 months before applying for the flat.
[LIST-ITEM] The flat must have a lease duration that covers the youngest buyer until they reach the age of 95. If the remaining lease is insufficient, the provided EHG will be prorated accordingly. Exceptions are made for buyers of 2-room Flexi flats on short leases.
[LIST-ITEM] You cannot own any private properties or land, whether locally or overseas. Additionally, you should not have disposed of any of these properties within the last 30 months.
[PARAGRAPH] Note that first-time single citizens purchasing a flat under the Single Singapore Citizen Scheme or Joint Singles Scheme are limited to only buying 2-room Flexi flats. Nonetheless, they can still take advantage of the EHG.
[HEADING-H2] How much Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) can I get?
[PARAGRAPH] According to the new property cooling measures 2024, eligible first-time families seeking new flats can now receive an EHG of up to S$120,000, while eligible first-time singles can benefit from an EHG (Singles) of up to S$60,000.
[PARAGRAPH] For eligible first-timer singles who buy a resale flat, they can receive up to $115,000 in housing grants comprising the revised EHG of up to $60,000, a CPF Housing Grant of up to $40,000, and a PHG of up to $15,000.
[PARAGRAPH] The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest updates and changes, you can check the official website.

[HEADING-H2] What is a unit or house number?
[PARAGRAPH] An assigned number, along with the street name, creates a distinct address for identification purposes.
[PARAGRAPH] A typical house address in Singapore consists of the [House Number], [Street Name], [# Unit Number, if applicable], and Singapore [Postal Code].
[HEADING-H2] What is a unit number application in Singapore?

[HEADING-H2] How to apply for a unit number in Singapore?

[HEADING-H2] What are the main things that must be considered when applying for a unit number?

[HEADING-H2] What is a Power of Attorney (POA)?
[PARAGRAPH] A Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal instrument in which one person delegates authority to another. It is often used for legal transactions like purchasing, selling, or renting real estate.
[PARAGRAPH] The donor is the individual who created the document, while the person authorised to act on behalf of the person granting the POA is called the donee.
[HEADING-H2] When to use the Power of Attorney (POA)?
[PARAGRAPH] A POA might be necessary if someone travels often, works overseas, or lives outside Singapore and cannot handle legal affairs, such as property sales, purchases, or rentals.
[HEADING-H2] How do I set up power of attorney in Singapore?
[HEADING-H2] What are the types of Power of Attorney (POA) available in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] The following are 5 types of POAs, each serving different purposes;
[PARAGRAPH] If the POA agreement does not clearly outline the donee’s authority in particular situations, then the general POA allows the donee to represent the donor in all cases.
[PARAGRAPH] With a general POA, the donee has the power to perform various tasks, such as engaging in legal and financial transactions, handling property, signing contracts for the donor, submitting tax returns, and other related duties.
[PARAGRAPH] A general POA remains effective unless it is cancelled in the following instances;
[LIST-ITEM] Revocation by the donor
[LIST-ITEM] Death of the donor
[LIST-ITEM] Incapacity of the donor
[LIST-ITEM] Or when a particular event is specified in the POA.
[PARAGRAPH] Under this type of POA, the donee is authorised to act on behalf of the donor but only in the designated areas. A special POA can be revoked in similar ways to a general POA.
[PARAGRAPH] An individual can use the LPA to give legal authority to a donee to manage their affairs in the case of a loss of mental capacity. In Singapore, the LPA is regulated by the Mental Capacity Act.
[PARAGRAPH] The LPA permits the donee to make decisions on behalf of the donor regarding their personal, financial, and property matters when the donor cannot do so. By having an LPA, the donor and their family can avoid potential uncertainty and issues arising from mental incapacity.
[PARAGRAPH] To ensure that the donor understands the purpose and consequences of the LPA, the certificate issuer must confirm that the LPA is valid and was created without any fraud, coercion, or undue pressure.
[PARAGRAPH] Follow these general steps to create an LPA:
[LIST-ITEM] Complete the LPA application by selecting a trusted donee who is at least 21 years old and specifying the powers to be granted.
[LIST-ITEM] Obtain certification from an LPA certificate issuer (E.g., a practising lawyer, a psychiatrist, or an accredited medical practitioner)
[LIST-ITEM] Submit the completed LPA application to the Office of the Public Guardian.
[PARAGRAPH] The Housing and Development Board (HDB) POA is the most common type of POA in Singapore. It is required when a homebuyer is unable to attend the appointment to collect their keys or appear in person for the signing of various documents, including;
[LIST-ITEM] Sales Contract
[LIST-ITEM] Lease Contract
[LIST-ITEM] Option to Purchase Agreement
[LIST-ITEM] Deed of Assignment
[LIST-ITEM] Lease in Escrow
[LIST-ITEM] and Mortgage in Escrow
[PARAGRAPH] Individuals located overseas who cannot sign legal documents in Singapore will also use HDB POAs, typically by hiring a lawyer to act on their behalf. The POA will outline the specific rights granted to the attorney, such as the authority to complete transactions, sign documents, and return funds to the CPF Board.
[PARAGRAPH] The Springing POA, also called the Conditional POA, is a type of POA that is activated only when a specific event occurs. During the creation of the POA, it is important to define the specific event that will trigger the activation of the POA. For example, the POA may grant authority to the donee only when the donor is located overseas.
[HEADING-H2] Can the Power of Attorney (POA) be revoked?
[PARAGRAPH] Yes, the POA can be terminated, especially if you are unsatisfied with the quality of service or results provided by your donee.
[PARAGRAPH] Prepare a revocation document and distribute copies to all relevant transaction entities, such as hospitals and banks. Your done should also receive an official copy of the revocation.
[HEADING-H2] How to keep your real estate investments running smoothly with Power of Attorney?
[PARAGRAPH] Choose the right agent
[PARAGRAPH] When establishing a power of attorney for your real estate, select a trustworthy agent familiar with your properties. This individual, often a spouse, adult child, or lawyer, should be willing to handle responsibilities such as rent collection, repairs approval, and managing property affairs.
[PARAGRAPH] Grant proper authority
[PARAGRAPH] Collaborate with an attorney to craft a comprehensive power of attorney document. This grants your agent legal authority for crucial tasks, including rent collection, maintenance approvals, lease signings, property management, financial transactions, and property sales.
[PARAGRAPH] Prevent abuse and misuse
[PARAGRAPH] Safeguard your interests by including provisions such as regular transaction accountings, restrictions on major decisions without prior approval, and nominating a successor agent. Work closely with your attorney to ensure proper recording, adhering to state requirements for real estate power of attorneys.
[PARAGRAPH] Maintain open communication
[PARAGRAPH] Keep your agent informed about all aspects of your real estate investments. Provide access to essential documents, contacts, and accounts, introducing them to tenants and property managers. Regular communication ensures readiness for potential emergencies and upholding your standards.

[HEADING-H2] Who is a Notary Public?
[PARAGRAPH] A Notary Public in Singapore is a qualified lawyer appointed by the Board of Commissioners for Oaths and Notaries Public to perform notarization of documents. These lawyers must meet certain criteria, such as being at least 40 years old and having a minimum of 15 years of legal experience.
[PARAGRAPH] The Notaries Public Act governs the activities of Notaries Public in Singapore.
[PARAGRAPH] To qualify as a Notary Public, individuals must be deemed “fit and proper persons” and currently practising advocates and solicitors in Singapore. Those who have declared bankruptcy, been struck off the advocates and solicitors’ roll, or found guilty of misconduct rendering them unsuitable for the role will have their appointments revoked.
[HEADING-H2] What does a Notary Public do?
[PARAGRAPH] The main role of a Notary Public is to witness, authenticate, and certify the execution of documents.
[PARAGRAPH] When you sign a document before a Notary Public, you are affirming the truthfulness of its information.
[PARAGRAPH] Their primary responsibility is to prevent fraud and ensure that individuals sign documents willingly and without coercion.
[HEADING-H2] Do I need a Notary Public?
[PARAGRAPH] Engaging a Notary Public becomes necessary when there is a legal requirement for notarization, and it is often a prerequisite when sending documents from Singapore to overseas entities.
[PARAGRAPH] Here are some instances where you might need to involve a Notary Public:
[LIST-ITEM] Verifying the signature and execution of documents like deeds, contracts, powers of attorney, incorporation papers, property transfers, Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) assignments, and other instruments to be used abroad. In business transactions, relevant parties may need to be present at the signing, and the Notary Public acts as a witness to ensure compliance with such requirements.
[LIST-ITEM] Administering oaths or affirmations for affidavits or statutory declarations, and attesting such documents.
[LIST-ITEM] Certifying true copies of documents such as passports and bank statements. The Notary Public verifies that the copies are genuine representations of the originals through a visual comparison.
[LIST-ITEM] Handling protests for bills of exchange, which are signed orders for payment. If the bill is dishonoured, the Notary Public can be involved in protesting the bill.
[LIST-ITEM] Recording a ship’s protest, a statement that protects shipowners and crew members from liability by attributing damages to maritime perils rather than negligence.
[PARAGRAPH] Even when notarization is not explicitly required, going through the notarization process can help reduce the risk of document forgery and assure business parties that the documents are authentic.

[HEADING-H2] What is redlining?
[PARAGRAPH] Redlining is a discriminatory practice in real estate, typically involving lenders that refuse to lend money or extend credit to borrowers in certain areas of a city. While redlining is illegal and not practiced in Singapore, understanding its implications is important for a global perspective on real estate.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding redlining
[PARAGRAPH] Redlining originated in the United States in the 1930s, when government-sponsored corporations created maps of urban areas, marking “risky” neighbourhoods in red. These areas, often home to racial or ethnic minorities, were then used by banks and insurance companies to deny or price services. This discriminatory practice led to a lack of investment in these neighbourhoods, contributing to their decline and perpetuating socio-economic disparities.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of redlining in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] While redlining is not practiced in Singapore, understanding this discriminatory practice can provide insights into the importance of fair lending practices and regulations in maintaining a healthy and inclusive real estate market. It underscores the need for regulations to prevent discrimination in lending and to ensure equal access to housing.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Redlining is a discriminatory practice that has shaped urban landscapes and perpetuated socio-economic disparities. While not practiced in Singapore, its history serves as a reminder of the importance of fair lending practices in real estate. It underscores the need for vigilance and regulation to ensure that everyone has equal access to housing opportunities.

[HEADING-H2] What is a Unique Entity Number (UEN) in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] A Unique Entity Number, or UEN, serves as the standard identification number for entities. Like how NRIC identifies Singapore citizens, the UEN uniquely identifies registered entities.
[HEADING-H2] What are the benefits of having a Unique Entity Number (UEN) in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Having a UEN simplifies your interactions with government agencies. Instead of using multiple numbers for different agencies, your UEN serves as a single identifier.
[PARAGRAPH] As a result, with your UEN, you can easily carry out tasks such as submitting corporate tax returns or requesting import and export licences.
[HEADING-H2] Who issues the UEN?
[PARAGRAPH] When you complete a registration process with the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA), a UEN will be automatically assigned to you as part of the standard procedure for incorporation or registration.
[HEADING-H2] Do I need a Unique Entity Number (UEN) in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] UEN will be provided to entities, including businesses, local companies, representative offices, LLPs, and societies that:
[LIST-ITEM] Engage in multiple interactions with government agencies.
[LIST-ITEM] Are recognised by a UEN Issuance Agency such as ACRA or ROS (Registry of Societies).
[PARAGRAPH] Here are some key points regarding UEN issuance:
[LIST-ITEM] Individuals will not be issued a UEN. Instead, they will use their NRIC numbers to interact with government agencies.
[LIST-ITEM] Entities with no or only occasional interactions with a single government agency, such as overseas companies making one-off sales to government agencies, will not be issued a UEN.
[LIST-ITEM] Sub-entities with branches and divisions of an entity will not be assigned a separate UEN.
[PARAGRAPH] For a comprehensive list of entity types eligible for UEN issuance and their corresponding UEN Issuance Agencies, refer to official websites.
