[HEADING-H2] What is bid in Singapore real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] A bid refers to the process of making an offer or proposal to purchase a property at an auction or through a competitive bidding process. Bidding allows potential buyers to compete with each other by offering different prices for the property they are interested in.
[PARAGRAPH] The highest bidder typically wins the auction and secures the property by agreeing to pay the bid amount. Bidding is a common method used in property auctions to determine the final selling price of a property based on the competitive offers made by interested buyers.
[HEADING-H2] How to craft a competitive construction bid and stand out from the crowd?
[PARAGRAPH] The construction industry is highly competitive. When bidding on a new project, it’s important to submit an attractive and accurate bid to stand out from other contractors. Follow these tips to craft a construction bid that gives you the best chance of winning the job.
[PARAGRAPH] Carefully review the project plans, specifications, and any other documents provided by the client. Make sure you fully understand the scope of work. Visit the job site to assess any access issues or other challenges. The more familiar you are with the project details, the more accurate your bid will be.
[PARAGRAPH] Calculate your direct construction costs like materials, labour, and equipment rental. Don’t forget to factor in overhead costs like insurance, bonding, permits, and project management. Build in a reasonable profit margin as well. Underestimating costs is one of the biggest mistakes contractors make.
[PARAGRAPH] Some clients award contracts purely based on lowest bid price. Others use a scored system that factors in things like experience, reputation, and project approach. Know what the client values most so you can tailor your bid accordingly.
[PARAGRAPH] Even if the bid process is anonymous, find ways to showcase what makes your company qualified. Provide examples of similar projects you’ve completed successfully. Demonstrate knowledge of the latest methods and building codes. Promote awards your firm has won.
[PARAGRAPH] Follow all instructions precisely. Use the required bid forms and format. Ensure all pricing and details are included. Double check for errors. Submit a neat, professional bid package that conveys competence.
[PARAGRAPH] If possible, establish rapport with the client before bidding by asking questions and offering solutions. Follow up after submitting your bid as well. The more familiar the client is with you, the better your chances.
[PARAGRAPH] With proper preparation, accurate estimating, and attention to what the client wants, you can submit competitive construction bids that get the results you want. Pay close attention to the details in the bidding process to stand out from the competition.

[HEADING-H2] What is tenancy-in-common?
[PARAGRAPH] Tenancy-in-common refers to a situation where multiple individuals share ownership of land or property, with each co-owner holding a specific portion. This share can vary from 30% to 70% or even 1% to 99%. Other unequal share arrangements are also possible and usually explicitly outlined in the property’s title deed.
[PARAGRAPH] This type of ownership arrangement is particularly suitable for property owners who are purchasing for investment purposes or for couples who plan to acquire another property in the near future.
[HEADING-H2] How does tenancy-in-common work?
[PARAGRAPH] Upon the co-owners demise, their ownership stake in the property is transferred to their beneficiaries. The transfer occurs either according to the provisions specified in the individual’s will or, in the absence of a will, under the Intestate Succession Act (Cap. 146).
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, Tenant 1 may possess a 60% share, while Tenants 2 and 3 hold 20% each. In the event of Tenant 1’s passing, the 60% ownership share in the property would be transferred to their beneficiaries, while the ownership stakes of Tenants 2 and 3 would remain unchanged.
[PARAGRAPH] This arrangement allows for a fair division of ownership interests and ensures that the property remains collectively owned even in the face of individual changes in ownership.
[HEADING-H2] How does Tenancy In Common differ from Joint Tenancy?
[PARAGRAPH] In Joint Tenancy, all co-owners have an equal interest in the property, and there exists a ‘right of survivorship.’ This means when one joint tenant dies, their share automatically passes to the surviving joint tenant(s). This is in stark contrast to TIC, where each owner’s stake may be unequal and does not have the right of survivorship.
[HEADING-H2] Popular Uses of Tenancy In Common in Singapore
[PARAGRAPH] While not as commonly mentioned as Joint Tenancy, TIC is prevalent in various scenarios:
[PARAGRAPH] Business Partnerships: Business partners might buy property as a joint investment but want flexibility in ownership based on their contribution.
[PARAGRAPH] Inheritance Planning: Families might use TIC to ensure property shares are distributed among heirs in specific ways.
[PARAGRAPH] Friends Buying Property Together: Friends who want to invest together but retain the freedom to sell or bequeath their share independently.
[HEADING-H2] How to Set Up Tenancy In Common in Singapore?
[HEADING-H2] Can You Convert from Joint Tenancy to Tenancy In Common (TIC)?
[PARAGRAPH] Yes, you can! If joint tenants decide that they’d rather have a TIC arrangement, they can make this change by executing a document called a ‘Declaration of Trust’ or through a process known as ‘severance.’
[HEADING-H2] What happens if a Tenant In Common wants to sell?
[PARAGRAPH] A TIC owner can sell their share without the consent of the other owners. However, they’re selling their percentage of the property, not a specific part. The buyer would step into the shoes of the selling tenant in common, inheriting all the rights and obligations of that share.
[HEADING-H2] What if there’s a disagreement among Tenants In Common?
[PARAGRAPH] In the event of disagreements that cannot be resolved, any tenant in common can apply for a court order to sell the property and distribute the proceeds. This process is known as “partitioning.”
[HEADING-H2] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Understanding Tenancy In Common and its implications is essential for anyone considering this form of property ownership in Singapore. It offers flexibility but also necessitates careful planning and clear communication among co-owners. If you’re considering TIC, it’s always wise to consult a property lawyer to ensure your interests are well protected.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Annual Value (AV) of the property?
[PARAGRAPH] A property’s Annual Value (AV) refers to the estimated annual rent that could be earned if the property was rented out, excluding maintenance costs and furniture.
[PARAGRAPH] The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) determines a property’s AV. To make these estimates, IRAS considers various factors such as the property’s size, condition, location, other relevant physical characteristics, and the rentals of comparable properties nearby.
[PARAGRAPH] It is worth noting that a property’s AV is determined by IRAS’ assessment criteria and not the actual rent earned by the property. The AV remains the same whether the property is vacant, rented, or owner-occupied.
[HEADING-H2] Why does IRAS use rentals rather than selling prices to calculate the Annual Value (AV)?
[PARAGRAPH] This is because there are usually more rental transactions than sales transactions, making it easier to obtain an accurate picture of market activity.
[PARAGRAPH] Rental price changes are also more predictable than sale price changes, which helps keep the property tax system more stable for property owners. Malaysia and Hong Kong also use a similar method to determine AV.
[PARAGRAPH] Additionally, it would be unfair to subsequent property owners to base AV on prior purchase prices, as costs of similar properties can change over time. This means newer property owners may have a higher AV if property prices rise.
[HEADING-H2] How to check the Annual Value (AV) of my property?
[HEADING-H2] Why is the Annual Value (AV) important?
[PARAGRAPH] Essentially, AV helps to determine how much tax you need to pay for your property.
[PARAGRAPH] If your property has a higher AV, you must pay more property tax. However, if you live on your property, you may pay a lower tax rate.
[HEADING-H2] When will IRAS update my property’s Annual Value (AV)?
[PARAGRAPH] IRAS checks the AV of properties each year to see if there are changes in the rental values of similar properties in the market.
[PARAGRAPH] The AV will be amended if the latest market rent data no longer supports your existing AV. If any changes are made to your property that could significantly affect its rental value, IRAS will adjust your AV from the change date.
[PARAGRAPH] Property owners will receive a Valuation Notice from IRAS, informing them of any AV changes, whether it has gone up or down, and when it will take effect.

[HEADING-H2] What is EBITDA?
[PARAGRAPH] Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation (EBITDA) is a measure of a company’s operating performance. In the context of real estate investment, it can provide insights into a property’s profitability before the influence of tax structure and financing
[HEADING-H2] Understanding EBITDA
[PARAGRAPH] EBITDA is calculated by adding back interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation to net income. This metric is often used by investors to compare the financial performance of different companies by eliminating the effects of financing and accounting decisions.
[PARAGRAPH] It’s a non-GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) financial figure, meaning it does not adhere to standard accounting rules used for financial reporting. As such, it’s often used in conjunction with other financial metrics for a more complete understanding of a company’s or property’s performance.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of EBITDA in Real Estate
[PARAGRAPH] In the real estate sector, EBITDA can be a useful tool for comparing the performance of different properties or real estate companies. It can provide a clearer picture of operational performance by focusing on earnings from core business operations, excluding interest, taxes, and non-cash expenses.
[PARAGRAPH] For instance, a real estate investor might use EBITDA to compare the profitability of two properties before considering the impact of their different financing structures or tax situations.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] EBITDA is a valuable metric for real estate investors, offering a measure of a property’s or a real estate company’s operational profitability. However, it should be used in conjunction with other financial metrics to get a comprehensive view of financial performance.
[PARAGRAPH] It’s important to note that while EBITDA can provide useful insights, it’s not a substitute for GAAP metrics and should not be used in isolation when making investment decisions.

[HEADING-H2] Is GST payable on the residential lease?
[PARAGRAPH] GST is not applicable on the sale and lease of residential properties.
[PARAGRAPH] However, non-residential properties are subject to GST. In cases where a property has residential and non-residential parts, only the non-residential portion is subject to GST.
[PARAGRAPH] When residential properties are furnished, GST should be charged on the supply of movable furniture and fittings. However, certain fixtures like built-in cabinets, wardrobes, kitchen and sanitary wares, and permanently attached wall-mounted air conditioners can be exempted from GST along with the property.

[HEADING-H2] What is abandonment?
[PARAGRAPH] Abandonment is the act of giving up the right to a property with no intention of returning. In Singapore’s real estate market, abandonment can have significant legal implications.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding abandonment
[PARAGRAPH] Abandonment involves the voluntary surrender of property, owned or rented, without naming a successor to own or rent it, and with the intention of not returning. In real estate, abandonment can refer to a homeowner who has left their property permanently and does not intend to return. It can also refer to a tenant who has left a rental property before the end of their lease without intending to return.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of abandonment in real estate and property
[PARAGRAPH] In the context of real estate, abandonment can have significant legal implications. For instance, a tenant who abandons a rental property before the end of their lease may still be liable for the remaining rent. Similarly, a homeowner who abandons their property may still be liable for mortgage payments, property taxes, and other obligations.
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Abandonment can have significant implications in real estate, affecting both landlords and tenants, as well as homeowners and lenders. Understanding the concept of abandonment can help individuals navigate these issues more effectively.
[PARAGRAPH] Nonetheless, dealing with abandonment can be complex, and it’s often advisable to seek legal advice.

[HEADING-H2] What is a property agent?
[PARAGRAPH] Also known as real estate salesperson (RES), property agents are licensed professionals who assist individuals in buying, selling, and renting real estate.
[PARAGRAPH] Their primary responsibility is to connect buyers and sellers, and they receive payment in the form of a commission, typically a percentage of the property’s sale price.
[PARAGRAPH] The RES can act on behalf of either the buyer or the seller.
[HEADING-H2] Should my property agent be registered with CEA?
[PARAGRAPH] The Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) requires all property agents in Singapore to be registered with their respective property agencies.
[PARAGRAPH] If the RES operates without a licence, they can be fined up to S$75,000 and imprisoned for up to three years. The client may also be affected if an unregistered agent causes any trouble.
[PARAGRAPH] You can easily verify if a property agent is CEA-registered by checking for their unique registration number. This would be a six-digit code with an alphabet at the front and back.
[PARAGRAPH] It’s important to note that property agents are prohibited by law from representing both buyers and sellers in a transaction due to potential conflicts of interest that can arise.

[PARAGRAPH] Treasury Bills (T-Bills) represent a widely favoured short-term investment vehicle in Singapore, particularly among cautious investors seeking a secure and low-risk means of augmenting their savings. With the full backing of the Singapore Government, T-Bills provide stability and consistent returns, thus holding an allure for conservative investors.
[HEADING-H2] Key features of T-Bills
[PARAGRAPH] Treasury Bills, commonly called T-Bills, are obtainable in two maturity periods: 6 months and one year. Unlike traditional bonds that make periodic interest payments, T-Bills are initially sold at a price lower than their face value and then redeemed at face value upon reaching maturity.
[PARAGRAPH] The variance between the purchase price and the face value constitutes the interest earned. For instance, a 6-month T-Bill issued in August 2024 offered a cut-off yield of 3.34% per annum.
[HEADING-H2] Investment requirements and process
[PARAGRAPH] T-Bills can be acquired through DBS, UOB, or OCBC bank platforms via online banking or in person at CPFIS agent bank branches.
[PARAGRAPH] When participating in T-Bills auctions, investors have the option to submit either competitive or non-competitive bids. In a competitive bid, an investor specifies the yield they are willing to accept. In contrast, in a non-competitive bid, the investor only specifies the amount to be invested without regard to the yield.
[PARAGRAPH] Non-competitive bids are typically prioritized, with up to 40% of the total issuance allotted.
[HEADING-H2] Benefits and considerations
[PARAGRAPH] Treasury Bills (T-Bills) present an opportunity for risk-free returns as they are guaranteed by the Singapore Government, thus offering a secure investment avenue. Furthermore, the interest income derived from T-Bills is exempt from tax for individual investors, presenting an added financial advantage.
[PARAGRAPH] Although T-Bills are not redeemable before maturity, their short tenors of 6 months or one year render them relatively liquid investments.
[HEADING-H2] Comparison with other investment options
[PARAGRAPH] Moreover, T-Bills offer analogous or marginally lower returns compared to fixed deposits. However, they boast lower minimum investment requirements and shorter lock-in durations.

[HEADING-H2] What is asset management in Singapore’s real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] Asset management in Singapore real estate involves the strategic management of properties and investments to optimise their value and performance. This includes overseeing the acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposition of real estate assets to meet the owner’s objectives.
[PARAGRAPH] How to maximise returns and mitigate risks with real estate asset management strategies?
[PARAGRAPH] Implementing a strategic asset management plan is key to optimising the performance of rental properties and mitigating risk exposure:
[HEADING-H2] 1. Conduct thorough tenant screening and underwriting
[PARAGRAPH] One of the biggest risks landlords face is ending up with a bad tenant who causes property damage or fails to pay rent on time. Conducting thorough tenant screening and underwriting during the leasing process is critical to assessing applicant risk and avoiding delinquencies. Run background checks, credit checks, verify income and rental history, and call references to carefully evaluate prospective tenants.
[PARAGRAPH] It’s also important to utilise tenant underwriting to confirm applicants meet minimum income and credit requirements. Setting appropriate occupancy standards minimises risk and helps attract responsible, reliable tenants.
[HEADING-H2] 2. Implement preventative maintenance programmes
[PARAGRAPH] Preventative maintenance helps preserve the physical and financial integrity of investment properties over time. Schedule regular unit inspections and tackle minor repairs immediately to prevent bigger, costlier issues down the road. Well-maintained properties also command higher rents and retain tenants longer.
[HEADING-H2] 3. Maintain adequate property reserves
[PARAGRAPH] Adequate cash reserves provide landlords with a financial safety net to handle unexpected vacancies, repairs, legal issues, and other unforeseen expenses that arise. The rule of thumb is to set aside 10-15% of gross rental income in a reserve account. This provides funds to smoothly handle crises without impacting cash flow.
[PARAGRAPH] For newer investors, aim to build up to the full 10-15% over time. Park reserve funds in a separate high-yield savings account so the money is easily accessible when needed.
[HEADING-H2] 4. Diversify your real estate portfolio
[PARAGRAPH] Concentrating investments in one geographic area or property type amplifies risk exposure. Economic shifts or natural disasters can devastate a concentrated portfolio. Diversifying real estate assets across different markets, building classes, and tenant demographics helps mitigate localised risks.
[HEADING-H2] 5. Work with a seasoned property management company
[PARAGRAPH] Handling day-to-day rental property management yourself may save money upfront, but also amplifies risks. Working with an experienced property management company acts as a risk mitigation strategy. Professional property managers specialise in areas like tenant relations, maintenance, rent collection, compliance, and leasing – allowing landlords to take a hands-off approach.
[PARAGRAPH] While fees do apply, the benefits gained from a property manager protecting your assets outweigh the costs. Their expertise also maximise operational efficiency.
[PARAGRAPH] Implementing these 5 essential real estate asset management strategies will help investors optimise returns while minimising risk exposure. Proactively managing properties using smart tenant screening, preventative maintenance, ample reserves, portfolio diversification, and professional property management sets up rentals for success.
[PARAGRAPH] With a strategic approach to asset management, real estate investors can maximise profits and mitigate risks over the long-term.

[HEADING-H2] What are boutique condos?
[PARAGRAPH] Boutique condo, or boutique condominium, is a smaller, exclusive development, offering privacy and unique features. These properties appeal to those who value privacy and serenity over large-scale living. While boutique condos have fewer amenities and smaller site areas than larger developments, they offer a unique living experience.
[HEADING-H2] Location
[PARAGRAPH] These condos are often located in quieter, more private areas, making them ideal for couples, empty nesters, or anyone seeking a more intimate living environment. The smaller community fosters stronger connections between neighbours, creating a sense of belonging.
[HEADING-H2] Features
[PARAGRAPH] A key feature of boutique condos is their flexibility in layout. Unlike larger condos built with prefabricated construction methods, boutique developments often allow for more freedom in interior design. This means homeowners can personalise their space more easily, whether by knocking down walls or opting for open-concept designs.
[PARAGRAPH] Additionally, many boutique condos are freehold properties, which means they come with perpetual ownership. This makes them a valuable long-term investment for Singaporeans.
[HEADING-H2] Affordability
[PARAGRAPH] Because these developments are on smaller plots of land, they are often more affordable than larger projects. The lower launch prices, however, do not necessarily mean lower future returns. While larger condos may experience faster price growth due to higher transaction volumes, boutique condos still offer solid investment potential.
[HEADING-H2] Pros of buying a boutique condo in Singapore
[PARAGRAPH] The biggest value-add when buying boutique condos is freehold ownership. Freehold properties offer perpetual ownership, meaning they are not subject to lease decay. This makes them a rare commodity, particularly in Singapore, where land is limited.
[PARAGRAPH] Freehold boutique condos can serve as valuable legacy assets, passing down wealth to future generations. This sense of security is attractive to those looking for a property that will retain its value over time and provide financial stability for their families.
[PARAGRAPH] Furthermore, boutique condos often come with a lower entry price compared to larger developments. Due to their smaller size and fewer amenities, developers can offer these properties at more affordable rates. This makes boutique condos an attractive option for buyers who want to invest in property without the premium costs associated with larger, more luxurious developments.
[PARAGRAPH] Last, but not the least, boutique condos offer privacy, exclusivity, and personalisation. With only a limited number of residents, these developments create a much more intimate and serene living environment. This exclusivity can be particularly appealing to individuals who prefer a quieter, more peaceful lifestyle.
[PARAGRAPH] Homeowners have the opportunity to knock down walls, create open-concept spaces, or personalise their homes to suit their needs. This is particularly attractive for buyers who want to create a bespoke living environment that reflects their individual style. Larger developments, on the other hand, often come with stricter renovation rules due to the use of prefabricated construction methods.
[HEADING-H2] Cons of choosing a boutique condo
[PARAGRAPH] One of the main disadvantages is the limited amenities offered. Larger developments often provide a wide range of facilities, such as gyms, pools, and communal spaces, which may be lacking in boutique condos. This can be a downside for residents who value these features or for families with young children who need access to recreational areas.
[PARAGRAPH] Many boutique condos are located in more private, less accessible areas. While this offers a sense of tranquillity and exclusivity, it may also mean that residents are further away from key amenities such as public transport, schools, and shopping centres. The more secluded nature of these developments may also affect daily commuting and overall accessibility.
[PARAGRAPH] Another potential concern is the lower liquidity of boutique condos. Smaller developments tend to have fewer buyers and lesser transaction volumes than larger developments, which may make it harder to sell a unit quickly. If you are looking for a property that can be easily resold, the limited number of units in boutique condos might pose a challenge.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Annual Percentage Rate (APR)?
[PARAGRAPH] The APR, or Annual Percentage Rate, refers to the yearly interest rate a person or organisation must pay for the privilege of borrowing money.
[PARAGRAPH] This rate is applied to various financial products, such as credit cards, car loans, and mortgages.
[PARAGRAPH] In other words, the APR tells you the total expense of borrowing money as a percentage of the loan’s original principal amount. The purpose of the APR on a loan or credit card is to provide an exact idea of the borrowing cost.
[PARAGRAPH] Hence, the APR is among the most important figures to consider when applying for new credit.
[HEADING-H2] What factors influence the Annual Percentage Rate (APR)?
[PARAGRAPH] The lender or creditor determines your APR, but it can also be affected by your credit scores.
[PARAGRAPH] For example, if you have a history of good credit behaviour and are viewed as a low-risk borrower by potential lenders and creditors, you may be offered a reduced interest rate, which typically leads to a lower APR.
[HEADING-H2] What is the difference between the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) and the interest rate?
[PARAGRAPH] APR and interest rate are similar in meaning, but they are not identical.
[PARAGRAPH] Interest rates only cover the cost of borrowing money and do not include any other expenses associated with the loan. It is expressed as a percentage and can be paid annually, monthly, or daily.
[PARAGRAPH] In contrast, the APR is the total interest rate charged for an entire year and includes additional costs associated with the loan. For example, a mortgage APR would typically reflect the interest rate and any closing costs, origination fees, broker fees, and other expenses related to obtaining a loan.
[PARAGRAPH] When comparing different loans, the APR gives borrowers a more comprehensive idea of the total costs involved. Due to this, the APR is generally higher than the interest rate, but this may vary from case to case.

[HEADING-H2] What is appreciation in Singapore real estate?
[PARAGRAPH] Appreciation in Singapore real estate refers to the increase in the value of a property over time. Capital appreciation occurs when you sell your property for a higher price than when you purchased it.
[PARAGRAPH] For example, if you buy an HDB 3-room for S$500,000 and sell it 5 years later for S$900,000, the capital appreciation is S$400,000. Similarly, if you buy a freehold condo at $800,000 and later sell it at S$1,000,000, the capital appreciation is S$200,000.
[HEADING-H2] What factors influence property appreciation in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Factors that can contribute to capital appreciation in Singapore real estate include:
[HEADING-H2] Tips on growing your property’s appreciation
[PARAGRAPH] If your objective is to transform real estate appreciation into lasting generational wealth, consider the following tips:
[PARAGRAPH] Start early and be consistent
[PARAGRAPH] Commence your real estate investment journey as early as possible to allow your properties ample time for appreciation. Initiate investments once you’ve accumulated sufficient savings for an initial rental property or flip. Consistency is crucial; continually augment your portfolio with new properties over the years, fostering equity growth and realising appreciation returns.
[PARAGRAPH] Reinvest profits
[PARAGRAPH] As your properties appreciate, reinvest a significant portion of your rental income and flip profits into acquiring new properties. The compounding effect in real estate can exponentially boost your portfolio and net worth over time.
[PARAGRAPH] Purchase cash-flowing rentals
[PARAGRAPH] While emphasising long-term property appreciation, acknowledge the importance of cash flow. Acquire rental properties in areas with robust tenant demand to minimise vacancy rates and enhance monthly cash flow, which can be reinvested. Cash flow acts as a financial cushion, especially during vacancies or necessary repairs.
[PARAGRAPH] Improve and maintain properties
[PARAGRAPH] Enhance your rental properties through upgrades and renovations. Initiating projects like kitchen and bathroom remodels, exterior facelifts, and system upgrades enables you to raise rents and boost property values. Consistent maintenance preserves curb appeal, retaining tenants for increased returns.
[PARAGRAPH] Utilise leverage
[PARAGRAPH] Optimise your purchasing power by leveraging rental property loans, lines of credit, and other financing tools. Although leveraging introduces risk, it enables the acquisition of more properties than feasible with personal capital alone, translating to greater appreciation potential over time.
[PARAGRAPH] Hold properties long-term
[PARAGRAPH] Resist the urge to sell properties prematurely. Prolonged ownership of real estate investments maximises appreciation potential. Holding onto properties over an extended period allows for optimal appreciation, facilitating the option to gift or sell at a reduced tax rate for intergenerational wealth transfer.

[HEADING-H2] What is Changi City Point?
[PARAGRAPH] Changi City Point is conveniently situated in the heart of Changi Business Park, providing direct access to Singapore Expo Station via the Downtown Line and the East-West Line.
[PARAGRAPH] Its prime location offers excellent connectivity to nearby residential areas such as Simei, Bedok, and Tampines. This includes private residential zones like Upper East Coast Road, Kew Drive, Tanah Merah, Upper Changi Road, and Bedok Road.
[HEADING-H2] What is in Changi CityPoint?
[PARAGRAPH] With more than 38 well-known shopping outlets, Changi City Point is a haven for shoppers seeking year-round discounts on various products, from renowned brands to sports items.
[PARAGRAPH] Visitors can enjoy a refreshing rooftop garden called “The Arena @ L3,” which features an outdoor amphitheatre, playground, and a trail with treehouses for children to explore.
[PARAGRAPH] Changi City Point boasts popular outlet stores like Coach Outlet, Nike Unite CCP, Adidas Outlet, PUMA Outlet, and prominent retailers such as Jollibee and FairPrice Finest. It also offers unique and enticing food and beverage concepts, including Hey Long Cha, ManNa Korean, Muyoo Bakery, The Dim Sum Place, and The White Tiffin.

[HEADING-H2] What amenities does Changi CityPoint have?
[LIST-ITEM] Customer service counter: The Customer Service Counter is on Level 2 and operates from 11 am to 9 pm. You can visit the counter during these hours for any assistance or inquiries. The counter also facilitates redemptions from 11 am to 9 pm.

[LIST-ITEM] Other services and facilities:
[PARAGRAPH] There are various services and facilities provided for your convenience at Changi City Point:

[LIST-ITEM] Free Mobile Charging Services: If your mobile device needs a quick recharge, you can use the free mobile charging services. This service is available on Level 2, next to the customer service counter, and operates from 10 am to 9.30 pm.
[LIST-ITEM] Bicycle parking bay: For cyclists, a dedicated bicycle parking bay is available on Level 1, next to the Oasis area (next to Canopy Changi City). This provides a convenient and secure space for parking your bicycle while you explore the mall.
[HEADING-H2] How to go to Changi CityPoint?
[PARAGRAPH] To get to Changi City Point, you have the convenience of shuttle buses operating on various routes. These shuttle buses operate from Monday to Friday, including public holidays, and run on a round-trip basis, ensuring easy, convenient travel to and from Changi City Point.
[PARAGRAPH] There are four routes in total, catering to different locations.
[LIST-ITEM] Route 1: This route operates from Monday to Friday, providing convenient transportation for those in the Changi South area.
[LIST-ITEM] Route 2: If you are coming from the SUTD campus or Simei MRT, this route operates on Saturdays and Sundays, ensuring convenient access to Changi City Point on weekends. However, this shuttle option is temporarily unavailable, be sure to check official websites for recent updates.

Tanjong Changi was the name given to Singapore’s extreme southeastern tip on Franklin and Jackson’s 1828 map. Vessels travelling through the Johor Straits would have to pass through Changi. Changi was also known as Franklin Point during early surveys of Singapore island from the 1820s to the 1830s after Captain Franklin was one of the early surveyors. It appeared that colonial authorities had given their name to Changi in addition to the existing Malay name.

[HEADING-H2] What is a statutory declaration in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] A statutory declaration is a formal statement to assert a particular matter’s truth.
[PARAGRAPH] Statutory declarations can be mandatory under certain legal requirements. However, individuals also have the option to voluntarily make a statutory declaration regarding any relevant issue.
[PARAGRAPH] Instances where a court may necessitate a statutory declaration include:
[PARAGRAPH] When submitting a statutory declaration, the person making the declaration is known as the declarant. The declarant needs to swear or affirm the truthfulness of the statutory declaration before a Commissioner for Oaths (CFO).
[HEADING-H2] How to prepare a statutory declaration in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Do not sign the statutory declaration before it has been sworn or affirmed. You are required to sign it in the presence of a CFO.
[HEADING-H2] How to swear or affirm a statutory declaration in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Once you have completed the statutory declaration form, you must swear or affirm it before a CFO. Information on arranging for CFO services can be obtained.
[PARAGRAPH] Subsequently, you may submit the sworn or affirmed statutory declaration to the relevant court overseeing your case.
[PARAGRAPH] Any changes, such as amendments or deletions, cannot be made to the declaration after it has been sworn or affirmed unless the changes are made in the presence of the CFO.
[HEADING-H2] What happens if a false statutory declaration is made in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Making a false statutory declaration is considered an offence. If found guilty, the following penalties may apply:
[LIST-ITEM] If false declarations are made in court proceedings, the potential consequences include a maximum sentence of 7 years of imprisonment and the imposition of a fine.
[LIST-ITEM] If false declarations are made for purposes other than for court use, the potential penalties involve a maximum penalty of 3 years of imprisonment and a fine.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the Singapore Land Authority (SLA)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Singapore Land Authority (SLA) is a statutory board operating under the Ministry of Law. It is a governmental organisation established by the Singapore Land Authority Act, which was formed through the merger of the Land Office, the Singapore Land Registry, the Survey Department, and the Land Systems Support Unit.
[PARAGRAPH] With the core mission of optimising land resources, the SLA aims to facilitate Singapore’s social and economic development by maximising the utilisation of land.
[PARAGRAPH] What does the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) do?
[PARAGRAPH] The SLA has a dual role, combining developmental and regulatory functions. In its developmental capacity, the SLA is responsible for:
[LIST-ITEM] Maintaining the national land information database.
[LIST-ITEM] Managing State land through land sales, leases, acquisitions, and allocations.
[LIST-ITEM] Developing and promoting the optimal utilisation of State properties for the public’s benefit.
[LIST-ITEM] Establishing geospatial data infrastructure and policies to facilitate knowledge creation and value generation for the Government, businesses, and the community.
[PARAGRAPH] As a regulatory entity, the SLA serves as Singapore’s national authority for land registration. It oversees property transactions’ registration and manages the national land survey system. Several divisions within the SLA handle legal and regulatory matters, including the Legal Division, Land Survey Division, Land Titles Registry, and Conveyancing Planning Unit.
[PARAGRAPH] The regulatory role of the SLA encompasses several crucial responsibilities:
[LIST-ITEM] Managing property registration by maintaining two land registers. This would be the Register of Deeds and the Land Titles Register.
[LIST-ITEM] Granting permissions for foreign ownership of properties as per the Residential Property Act.
[LIST-ITEM] Regulating property boundary surveys, known as cadastral surveys, conducted by Registered Surveyors.
[LIST-ITEM] Overseeing the regulation of rental, sale, and purchase transactions involving State properties under the State Lands Act.
[LIST-ITEM] Making vacant State land available to the public for community use when immediate development is not required.
[PARAGRAPH] The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, head over to the official website.

[HEADING-H2] What is equity?
[PARAGRAPH] The amount you owe on loans that are backed by real estate plus its current market value equals equity. To simplify things further, think of equity as being what belongs exclusively to an individual with regards to their property – once all outstanding debts have been paid off this figure is calculated.
[HEADING-H2] Factors influencing equity and the process of utilising it
[PARAGRAPH] Various factors can alter the equity in a given property, but repayment of the outstanding money borrowed for a mortgage loan enhances home-buyer’s equity. Your property’s changing market value should also be considered as a factor, as the worth of the property rises so does its corresponding equity.
[PARAGRAPH] You may want to explore options like a home equity loan or term loan if you need ready access to cash using your property’s value as collateral, and your ability to borrow money is expanded due to these financial products which allow using your home’s equity.
[HEADING-H2] Comparing equity with other property-related concepts
[PARAGRAPH] It is common to compare equity with concepts like mortgage and property value, whereas the real ownership stake in a property is represented by its equity.
[HEADING-H2] Advantages and disadvantages of utilising equity
[PARAGRAPH] Equity utilisation provides an opportunity for homeowners to get larger loans with lower interest rates by securing it against their property, so if you have large expenses such as renovating a house or starting a business you can use this to finance them.
[PARAGRAPH] The primary disadvantage here is placing your home on the line as collateral, in case you are incapable of repaying back the loan amount then there is a threat of facing foreclosure in which lenders take hold of your property.
[HEADING-H2] Types of equity loans
[HEADING-H3] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] Looking back, equity emerges as an indispensable asset in meeting fundamental monetary requirements. However, understanding the risks involved and carefully assessing your financial situation is important before deciding whether or not borrowing against your home equity is right for you.

[PARAGRAPH] A Joint Venture (JV) is a business arrangement where two or more parties agree to pool their resources for a specific project or business activity. In Singapore’s real estate sector, JVs commonly involve developers, investors, and landowners combining their expertise and capital to undertake property development projects.
[HEADING-H2] Key laws and regulations
[PARAGRAPH] Joint ventures in Singapore are governed by a combination of contract law, company law, and specific real estate regulations. Let’s go over these in detail:
[PARAGRAPH] 1. Contract Law:
[PARAGRAPH] The foundation of a JV is the Joint Venture Agreement. This contract outlines the rights, obligations, and responsibilities of each party. Key aspects include profit and loss sharing, management roles, dispute resolution, and exit strategies. The Contract Act governs the enforceability of these agreements.
[PARAGRAPH] 2. Company Law:
[PARAGRAPH] Often, a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) – a separate company – is formed for the real estate joint venture. This is governed by the Companies Act, which dictates company registration, shareholder rights, and directors’ duties. This allows each party to maintain their individual corporate identity while still engaging in the venture.
[PARAGRAPH] 3. Land Titles (Strata) Act:
[PARAGRAPH] The Land Titles (Strata) Act in Singapore is a crucial piece of legislation that governs the ownership and management of strata-titled properties. These are properties where multiple owners share common areas, such as condominiums, apartments, and some commercial buildings.
[PARAGRAPH] The Act’s primary purpose is to provide a legal framework for the subdivision of land and buildings into strata titles, enabling individual ownership of units within a larger development. It sets out the rights and responsibilities of strata title owners, the management of common property, and the resolution of disputes. It applies to all strata-titled developments in Singapore, both residential and commercial.
[PARAGRAPH] 4. Planning Act:
[PARAGRAPH] The Planning Act in Singapore is a cornerstone of the country’s urban development, providing the legal framework for land use planning and control. The Planning Act’s primary purpose is to regulate and control the development of land in Singapore, ensuring that it aligns with the country’s long-term planning objectives. The Act empowers the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) to formulate and implement land use plans, guiding the physical development of Singapore.
[PARAGRAPH] In any real estate joint venture, all parties are expected to comply with zoning regulations and planning permissions obtained from the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA). Any deviations require approvals and may impact the project’s feasibility.
[PARAGRAPH] 5. Building Control Act:
[PARAGRAPH] This Act ensures building safety and standards. All joint ventures must adhere to regulations set by the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) for design, construction, and maintenance of buildings. This includes obtaining necessary building permits and certificates of statutory completion.
[PARAGRAPH] 6. Stamp Duties Act:
[PARAGRAPH] Stamp duties are payable on property transactions. JVs must account for stamp duties on land transfers, share transfers, and other relevant transactions. The amount payable varies depending on the type of property and the transaction value.
[PARAGRAPH] 7. Foreign Ownership Restrictions:
[PARAGRAPH] For any real estate joint ventures involving foreign entities, restrictions on foreign ownership of certain types of land (e.g., landed properties) apply. These are governed by the Residential Property Act and require approvals from the Singapore Land Authority (SLA).

[HEADING-H2] What is the SOP Act?
[PARAGRAPH] Often, contractors and subcontractors are unable to endure delayed payments and pay their own subcontractors or suppliers for completed work, due to a lack of economies of scale. Moreover, if there are any delays in completing the project, the principal contractors may be held responsible for substantial liquidated damages, typically calculated per day.
[PARAGRAPH] As such, the Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment (SOP) Act entered into force on April 1, 2005.
[PARAGRAPH] The Act intends to enhance cash flow in the built environment industry by allowing parties to request progress payments for completed construction work and any additional items and services provided during the construction project.
[PARAGRAPH] It also offers a low-cost adjudication system for resolving payment issues.
[HEADING-H2] Who benefits from the SOP Act?
[PARAGRAPH] The SOP Act is beneficial to the following groups;
[LIST-ITEM] Contractors, including both principal and supporting contractors
[LIST-ITEM] Suppliers who provide materials for a specific construction project in Singapore
[LIST-ITEM] Consultants who offer advice for a particular building project in Singapore
[LIST-ITEM] Homeowners
[LIST-ITEM] Developers
[HEADING-H2] How does the SOP Act help firms in the construction industry?
[PARAGRAPH] The SOP Act supports businesses in the built environment industry by providing the following benefits:
[LIST-ITEM] Guaranteeing the right to payment for those who provide goods or services for construction projects in Singapore, excluding any “pay when paid” or “pay if paid” contract clauses.
[LIST-ITEM] Setting up default (statutory) payment arrangements without any contractual payment obligations.
[LIST-ITEM] Claimants can request adjudication if they do not receive a payment response or the full amount they are owed.
[LIST-ITEM] Allowing the claimant to cease work or provision of services if the respondent does not pay the amount determined by adjudication.
[LIST-ITEM] Providing additional options such as the ability to place a lien on goods and to execute an adjudication decision as a judgement debt.
[HEADING-H2] What should I know about the SOP Act?
[PARAGRAPH] Contracts for the refurbishment of HDB apartments, for example, when no structural work is required, are not covered by the Act.
[HEADING-H2] What are the proper procedures for a claimant to submit a valid payment claim?
[PARAGRAPH] Ensuring that the payment claim adheres to the terms outlined in the contract and the relevant legislation is important.
[PARAGRAPH] As per the contract terms, you are entitled to submit a payment claim, which should be served by the final day of the following month after the contract is made or any subsequent month if no terms are specified.

[PARAGRAPH] In the context of Singapore’s intricate real estate market, the term ‘Red Herring’ might surface, especially in relation to property investment. A Red Herring is a preliminary prospectus filed by a company with securities regulators, usually containing information about the company and its upcoming public offering. In a broader sense, it can also refer to a misleading clue or distraction that is meant to divert attention away from the real issue.
[HEADING-H2] Understanding red herring
[PARAGRAPH] In real estate, a Red Herring might refer to information that, while somewhat related to the property, is used to distract a buyer from a potential issue or to steer negotiations in a certain direction. For example, a seller might emphasise the potential for future development in a neighbourhood to divert attention from current issues with a property.
[HEADING-H2] Importance of recognising a red herring in real estate
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore’s competitive property market, being able to identify a Red Herring is crucial for several reasons:
[PARAGRAPH] Focused decision making: Buyers need to separate the core facts that should influence their decision from unrelated or secondary information that might be serving as a distraction.
[PARAGRAPH] Negotiation strategy: For both buyers and sellers, understanding when a Red Herring is being used can help in formulating a more effective negotiation strategy.
[PARAGRAPH] Risk mitigation: Recognising a Red Herring allows buyers to focus on the essential aspects of a property, potentially avoiding unforeseen issues after the purchase.
[PARAGRAPH] Legal and ethical boundaries: While using a Red Herring might be a tactic in negotiations, it is important for sellers and agents to maintain transparency and avoid crossing into misrepresentation.
[HEADING-H2] Conclusion
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore’s dynamic real estate market, where every transaction is significant, understanding the concept of a Red Herring is essential. Buyers should be vigilant and focused on the critical aspects of a property, not allowing unrelated information to cloud their judgment.
[PARAGRAPH] Sellers, while aiming to present their property in the best light, should maintain ethical standards and avoid using misleading tactics.

[PARAGRAPH] If you own a private property in Singapore, you might have the option to tap into its value through a home equity loan. This type of loan allows you to borrow money using your property as collateral, giving you access to a significant sum based on your home’s current market value. What’s even more convenient is that you can apply for this loan even if you are still paying off your existing mortgage.
[PARAGRAPH] But is leveraging your home’s equity a good idea? While this financing option can be useful in certain situations, it’s important to understand how it works before deciding if it’s the right fit for your financial needs.
[HEADING-H2] What are Home Equity Loans in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Home equity loans go by different names, such as cash-out refinancing or property equity financing, but they all function in a similar way. Essentially, they allow homeowners to borrow against the portion of their home they own outright. However, there’s a catch – you must use your property as collateral, meaning the lender has the right to repossess it if you fail to repay the loan.
[PARAGRAPH] Since the loan amount is based on your accumulated equity, the more your property has appreciated in value, the more you may be able to borrow.
[HEADING-H2] What are the eligibility and restrictions for Home Equity Loans in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Not all properties qualify for home equity loans. If you own an HDB flat, this financing option isn’t available to you. Home equity loans are strictly for private property owners.
[PARAGRAPH] Additionally, banks tend to be more willing to approve these loans for fully paid properties, as they carry lower risk. If you still have an outstanding mortgage, your eligibility and loan amount will depend on how much equity you’ve built up over time.
[HEADING-H2] What is the Home Equity Loan amount and limits?
[PARAGRAPH] While it may seem like you can borrow against the full value of your home, that’s not the case. The maximum loan amount is determined after deducting any outstanding mortgage and CPF funds used for the property’s purchase.
[PARAGRAPH] In general, banks follow a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, which is usually capped at 75% of your remaining equity. Additionally, borrowers must meet regulatory limits like the Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR), which ensures they don’t take on more debt than they can afford.
[HEADING-H2] What are the costs and time involved to get a Home Equity Loan in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] Applying for a home equity loan isn’t an instant process. One of the first steps involves getting your property professionally valued, which can cost a few thousand dollars.
[PARAGRAPH] After that, you’ll need to wait for the bank’s approval. This entire process can take up to two months, so it’s not the best option if you need funds urgently.

[HEADING-H2] What is cluster housing?
[PARAGRAPH] In Singapore, a cluster house is a type of housing that combines elements of different housing schemes. It consists of homes that are uniform in size, design, and area.
[PARAGRAPH] Comparable to condos, cluster homes are often located within gated communities and are inhabited by residents seeking convenience, security, and seclusion. These communities also offer exclusive amenities and facilities like swimming pools, gyms, and parking spaces.
[PARAGRAPH] Cluster housing typically features two to three floors and can be terrace houses, semi-detached houses, or bungalows.
[HEADING-H2] Condominium vs cluster housing – What’s the difference?
[PARAGRAPH] Although condos and cluster homes are designed for a community of homeowners and residents, they are entirely different.
[PARAGRAPH] Condos are usually situated in tall buildings or towers, while cluster homes are constructed to resemble landed properties, providing residents with greater privacy and living space.
[HEADING-H2] Townhouse vs cluster housing – What’s the difference?
[PARAGRAPH] Townhouse properties are typically linked by shared walls, connecting all neighbours.
[PARAGRAPH] In contrast, cluster house properties are constructed and arranged to provide each resident with a plot of land and personal living space, offering greater privacy.
[HEADING-H2] Salient features of cluster housing
[PARAGRAPH] One of the main features of a cluster house property is its high potential for financial gain.
[PARAGRAPH] According to a 2015 report by SLP International, the capital values of cluster homes have risen faster than those of conventional landed properties.
[PARAGRAPH] In addition, cluster homes have been found to generate substantial rental income similar to that of landed homes. Investing in a cluster home can offer owners significant financial returns when renting or selling the property.
[PARAGRAPH] Cluster house properties provide residents with the advantages of both landed properties and condominiums, including 24/7 security and access to communal facilities.
[PARAGRAPH] These homes are designed to resemble landed properties, providing residents with a private living space while offering access to modern condominium amenities. This allows residents to enjoy the best of both worlds at a more affordable price than owning all these features in a single living space.
[PARAGRAPH] Cluster houses have lower maintenance costs since a developer manages all maintenance and upkeep duties, including repairing and renovating communal facilities like swimming pools, gyms, and parking spaces.
[PARAGRAPH] The developer is also responsible for repainting the cluster house’s exterior and repairing any damages to the property’s exterior.

[HEADING-H2] What is the Staggered Downpayment Scheme?
[PARAGRAPH] HDB’s Staggered Downpayment Scheme is a payment arrangement that allows individuals to split their downpayment into two installments when purchasing a property.
[PARAGRAPH] Through this scheme, a portion of the downpayment is made upon signing the Agreement for Lease, which signifies the commitment to purchase the property. The remaining balance of the downpayment is paid at the key collection when the buyer takes possession of the property.
[PARAGRAPH] This scheme offers flexibility and helps reduce financial burdens by allowing homebuyers to manage their cash flow more effectively throughout the property acquisition process.
[HEADING-H2] What are the eligibility requirements for the Staggered Downpayment Scheme?
[PARAGRAPH] The Staggered Downpayment Scheme applies to two categories of flat buyers:
[LIST-ITEM] They must have booked an uncompleted flat with 5 rooms or a smaller size through any of HDB’s sales exercises.
[LIST-ITEM] Both applicants must be first-timers, or the couple must consist of a first-timer and a second-timer applicant.
[LIST-ITEM] The flat application must have been submitted on or before the younger applicant’s 30th birthday.
[PARAGRAPH] Flat owners can qualify for the Staggered Downpayment Scheme if they meet the following conditions:
[LIST-ITEM] They have booked an uncompleted 3-room or smaller flat in a non-mature estate through any HDB sales exercises.
[LIST-ITEM] They have not sold or finalised the sale of their existing flat at the time of their new flat application.
[HEADING-H2] Additional Reading

[HEADING-H2] What is the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS)?
[PARAGRAPH] The Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) represents the monthly payouts during retirement that cover essential living expenses.
[PARAGRAPH] The BRS is one of three tiers within the CPF Retirement Sum framework, with the other two being the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) and the Full Retirement Sum (FRS). The BRS is the lowest tier compared to others, designed to provide a baseline level of financial security.
[PARAGRAPH] When individuals turn 55, their CPF savings up to the BRS are set aside in their Retirement Account (RA). These savings are then utilised to generate monthly payouts through the CPF LIFE (Lifelong Income for the Elderly) scheme, starting at 65 or a chosen later age.
[PARAGRAPH] If your CPF balance meets the BRS requirement at the age of 55 and you do not own any property, you can withdraw S$5,000 monthly.
[PARAGRAPH] However, if an individual owns a property with sufficient lease remaining until the age of 95 or older, they have the flexibility to meet their BRS using a combination of property and cash. This enables them to withdraw a portion of their RA savings to the BRS using their property. Individuals can access a larger amount for withdrawal from their CPF accounts by opting to pledge their property.
[PARAGRAPH] By adhering to the BRS, CPF guarantees that future retirees will get adequate monthly payouts to cover all their essential needs and maintain financial security.
[HEADING-H2] How much money will I receive from the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) in 2025?
[HEADING-H2] What are the key things you need to know about the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS)?
[PARAGRAPH] In the case of joint ownership of a property, the amount that can be pledged is limited to the individual’s share of the house.
[PARAGRAPH] The purpose of pledging the property is to ensure that the value of the assets contributes towards meeting the FRS requirement. [HEADING-H2] What is the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)?
[PARAGRAPH] Upon reaching age 55, Singaporean and Permanent Resident (PR) CPF members will have a Retirement Account (RA) established for them.
[PARAGRAPH] The funds from their Ordinary Account (OA) and Special Account (SA) will be used to finance the RA, up to the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) limit. The balance in the RA will continue to accrue interest until it is transferred into the CPF Life Scheme at the age of 65.
[PARAGRAPH] The savings in the RA play an essential role in determining the monthly CPF Life payment and overall CPF balances.
[PARAGRAPH] CPF has established three target amounts, namely the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), Full Retirement Sum (FRS), and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS), to ensure that Singaporeans are saving sufficiently for their retirement.
[HEADING-H2] How does the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) work?
[PARAGRAPH] The ERS is a little bit different from the BRS and FRS as it represents the upper limit for topping up your RA and determines the maximum CPF Life payouts you can receive. Upon reaching age 55, you become eligible to contribute funds to your RA up to the ERS, provided that you meet its threshold.
[PARAGRAPH] In 2023, the ERS threshold is set at S$298,200, reflecting the target amount for a secure and comfortable retirement.
[PARAGRAPH] According to CPF, the ERS is set at three times the BRS, resulting in significantly higher CPF Life payouts. For individuals with surplus funds intended for retirement, it can be advantageous to allocate these funds toward meeting the ERS in their RA.
[HEADING-H2] Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) vs Full Retirement Sum (FRS) vs Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) – Which is the best fit for you?
[PARAGRAPH] Achieving the FRS guarantees a reliable monthly income through CPF Life payouts, ensuring a comfortable standard of living during retirement. On the other side, meeting the BRS may require exploring options like downsizing one’s property to adequately fund retirement expenses.
[PARAGRAPH] For those who desire a higher level of financial security and wish to enjoy a more luxurious retirement, aiming for the ERS is recommended.

[HEADING-H2] What is a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] The Rental Tenancy Agreement is a contract that outlines the terms and conditions of a rental property, including clauses that protect the interests of both landlords and tenants. It covers key aspects of the tenancy, such as monthly rent, maintenance and repairs, and privacy.
[PARAGRAPH] In case of disputes or disagreements, the Tenancy Agreement serves as a point of reference for both parties.
[HEADING-H2] What should be included in a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] The agreement should clearly state the property being rented and the duration of the tenancy. It should also specify the payment of rent and utilities, including any additional charges, subscriptions, or license fees.
[PARAGRAPH] The tenant may be required to provide a security deposit, which may be forfeited if the property is damaged or the tenant violates the terms of the agreement. The agreement should also outline the permitted use of the premises and require appropriate upkeep of the property.
[PARAGRAPH] The tenant’s covenants, such as paying rent and keeping the property in good repair, should also be included, along with the landlord’s covenants, such as providing a habitable dwelling and ensuring quiet enjoyment of the property.
[PARAGRAPH] Termination of the lease, suspension of rent, notices, anticipatory breach, and stamp fees are important clauses that should also be included in the agreement.
[HEADING-H2] What is the process of the payment and signing of the Tenancy Agreement in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] To secure a rental property, tenants typically need to pay a deposit equal to one month’s rent for a one-year lease or two month’s rent for a two-year lease, along with the first month’s rent. It’s advisable not to pay more than one month’s rent as a deposit.
[PARAGRAPH] A third-party witness, such as an agent, should witness the signing of the tenancy agreement.
[PARAGRAPH] Both parties should agree on a fixed payment method, such as GIRO or internet banking, to ensure proper documentation of all financial transactions. It is also recommended to avoid making cash payments for the deposit or rent unless necessary. Instead, cheques should be used as proof of payment.
[HEADING-H2] Where do I get a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore?
[PARAGRAPH] While some clauses may require customisation, most are ready for use.

[HEADING-H2] What is an SG Arrival Card?
[PARAGRAPH] The SG Arrival Card (SGAC), also known as the white card or paper disembarkation/embarkation (DE) card, is the electronic equivalent of the paper form foreign visitors use to fill out upon arrival in Singapore for immigration clearance.
[PARAGRAPH] On March 27, 2020, the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA) discontinued using the paper DE card, requiring all travellers to provide their arrival information through an “SG Arrival Card” e-Service instead.
[PARAGRAPH] Every traveller must complete the SGAC declaration within a maximum of 3 days before their arrival. This ensures smooth immigration clearance without unnecessary delays.
[PARAGRAPH] The only exception to this rule is for Singapore Citizens, Permanent Residents, and Long-Term Pass Holders who enter Singapore through land checkpoints, as they are not required to fill in the SGAC declaration.
[HEADING-H2] How to submit an SG Arrival Card?
[PARAGRAPH] Use the official channels to submit your SG Arrival Card.
[PARAGRAPH] You can do this through the official ICA website or the “MyICA” mobile application, which is available for free download from the App Store (iOS) or Google Play (Android).
[PARAGRAPH] The submission of the SG Arrival Card through the official e-Service is free of charge.
[PARAGRAPH] Be cautious of phishing sites if you submit the card through unofficial platforms. The ICA does not endorse or support any commercial entities that offer paid assistance for submitting the SG Arrival Card.
[HEADING-H2] What is an electronic health declaration?
[PARAGRAPH] As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, Singapore has implemented a mandatory health declaration, which will be obtained along with the arrival card. The health declaration should be included in the SGAC e-submission.
[HEADING-H2] Who is required to complete the electronic health declaration?
[PARAGRAPH] All individuals entering Singapore, including Residents (Singapore citizens, Permanent Residents, Long-Term Pass holders, travellers enrolled in the Frequent Traveler Program, and foreign visitors) must submit a health declaration as part of the SGAC submission.
[PARAGRAPH] Long-Term Pass holders encompass individuals holding a Student’s Pass, Dependant’s Pass, Long-Term Visit Pass, or Work Pass.
[PARAGRAPH] This requirement does not apply to those who are transiting or transferring through Singapore without undergoing immigration clearance or Residents entering via Land Checkpoints.
[HEADING-H2] Is the SG Arrival Card the same as a visa?
[PARAGRAPH] The SG Arrival Card should not be treated as a visa. It does not authorise to enter Singapore or guarantee entry into the country.
[PARAGRAPH] Even if an individual has obtained an SG Arrival Card, they must still comply with any applicable visa requirements before entering Singapore.

[HEADING-H2] Don’t get burned: Why property insurance is a must-have for every homeowner
[PARAGRAPH] As a homeowner, securing property insurance is one of the most crucial steps you can take. It may seem like an added expense at first, but the long-term benefits and protections it offers are invaluable. Let’s delve into why property insurance is essential for every homeowner.
[HEADING-H3] Protect your investment
[PARAGRAPH] Your home is likely the largest investment you’ll ever make. The time, money, and effort you’ve invested in acquiring your home can be jeopardised by unforeseen events. Fires, storms, floods, and theft can cause significant damage or total loss. Property insurance offers peace of mind, safeguarding your financial investment against these unpredictable calamities.
[HEADING-H3] Avoid massive out-of-pocket expenses
[PARAGRAPH] Damage to your property can lead to enormous repair costs. Simple repairs for water damage or replacing personal belongings can quickly amount to thousands of dollars. Without insurance, these expenses come out of your pocket. Property insurance covers the majority of these costs, preventing the need to drain your savings or incur debt.
[HEADING-H2] Get replacement cost coverage
[PARAGRAPH] Your policy must include replacement cost coverage. This coverage pays for rebuilding your home with similar quality materials if it’s destroyed. The land may retain some value, but the cost of rebuilding can be staggering. Replacement cost coverage ensures you can rebuild without suffering a major financial loss.
[HEADING-H3] Protect yourself from liability
[PARAGRAPH] Home insurance isn’t just about protecting your property; it’s also about protecting yourself. Liability coverage is crucial if someone gets injured on your property and decides to sue. This can include slip and fall incidents or injuries caused by defects in your home. Liability coverage provides a buffer against legal fees and damages, protecting your financial well-being.
[HEADING-H3] Safeguard yourself against disasters
[PARAGRAPH] Disasters like fires, storms, and floods might seem distant until they happen to you. Being unprepared for such events can lead to total loss. Property insurance is your primary defence against these disasters. Ensure your coverage limits are adequate to protect your home’s value.
[PARAGRAPH] Property insurance provides essential financial security for homeowners. It’s a protective measure that shouldn’t be overlooked or delayed. By securing a comprehensive insurance policy, you protect your home, belongings, and financial stability. Don’t wait until disaster strikes – get insured now to avoid the potentially devastating consequences of being unprotected.

[PARAGRAPH] What is the Building and Construction Authority (BCA)?

It was established in 1999 through the merger of the Construction Industry Development Board (CIDB) and the Building Control Division of the Public Works Department (PWD).

[PARAGRAPH] Through initiatives like the BCA Academy, which offers tailored training courses for construction personnel at different levels, the BCA ensures that the sector’s talent is equipped with the necessary skills and knowledge.
[PARAGRAPH] The BCA oversees and regulates Singapore’s building industry to ensure that buildings are designed, constructed, and maintained to meet high safety standards. This includes buildings and areas such as excavation works, amusement rides, lifts, escalators, exterior features, and outdoor advertisement signs.
[PARAGRAPH] The BCA is a strong advocate for sustainability in the built environment. It has gained international recognition through initiatives like the BCA Green Mark scheme, which promotes green buildings, reduces carbon footprint, and conserves resources.

[PARAGRAPH] The BCA works closely with industry stakeholders to promote sustainable construction practices. By adopting environmentally friendly approaches, the industry can minimise the environmental impact of construction activities and contribute to a more sustainable built environment.
[PARAGRAPH] The BCA strives to create an inclusive society by improving accessibility for people of all abilities. It establishes guidelines such as the Code on Accessibility in the Built Environment and advocates for Universal Design, ensuring that buildings, products, and environments are accessible to everyone.

[HEADING-H2] What is in Jurong Point?
